title: 'A complete surprise' - XDS-Astana respond to Harold Tejada biological passport abnormalities
author: Katy Madgwick
text:
XDS-Astana have responded to the news that Harold Tejada is under investigation by the International Testing Agency (ITA), following suspected abnormalities in his biological passport.

It was revealed on Friday, November 27, that Netcompany-Ineos had terminated their contract with Tejada following the news that the 29-year-old from Colombia had been notified of an anti-doping rule violation over the alleged use of a prohibited substance or method, following unexplained abnormalities in his biological passport.

Tejada enjoyed success in 2026 at Paris-Nice, winning stage 6, and was second in a stage at the Tour de France, before recording a top-10 finish at the Vuelta a España later in the summer.

He was due to transfer from XDS-Astana to Netcompany-Ineos in January 2027. He remains under contract with XDS-Astana until December 31.

“This came as a complete surprise to the team,” XDS Astana said in a statement also issued on Friday, November 27.

“In accordance with the disciplinary procedure before the ITA/UCI, the rider will be given an opportunity to present his defense and/or to accept the violation and a sanction. The team is not part of these proceedings. It is now for the relevant authorities to assess the case.

“The team has a zero-tolerance policy with respect to doping practices, and it supports the UCI/ITA efforts to fight against doping in the sport of cycling.”

Astana confirmed that Tejada had been suspended from the team, effective immediately.

Tejada has spent his entire professional career at the Kazakh team, turning pro with them in 2020 and remaining for some seven seasons. His results gradually improved, from a stage win at the 2019 Tour de l'Avenir, which underscored his considerable climbing potential, to a victory on home soil at the 2024 Tour of Colombia, and finally his first WorldTour stage win at the 2026 Paris-Nice.

Tejada released a statement on Friday, maintaining his innocence and stating his intention to cooperate with the investigation process. "From day one, I have acted with diligence and responsibility, providing all requested information in a timely manner. I will continue to do so throughout the entire process, with full respect for the anti-doping authorities and cycling institutions."

title: Two Médecins Sans Frontières staff killed by Israeli strike in Gaza, charity says
author: William Christou
text:
MSF and head of WHO denounce attack on Gaza City clinic as Israel claims security guards were members of Hamas

Israeli forces have bombed a clinic run by Médecins Sans Frontières in Gaza City, killing two of its staff members, the organisation has said.

MSF said Israel directly struck the clinic, despite the fact that its location was known to the Israeli military and that it was well marked with MSF logos. The organisation denounced the attack and said that with the deaths of the two security guards on Saturday, Israel had killed 17 of its staff members during the war in Gaza.

The head of the World Health Organization , Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, condemned the bombing, saying: “Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked.”

“Attacks on health facilities, health workers and humanitarian personnel in Gaza are outrageous and unacceptable … These attacks MUST STOP,” Ghebreyesus said in a post on X.

The Israeli military claimed that the two men whom they killed, Ahmad Abou Hassira and Moaz Alitsbach, were members of Hamas’s military wing. It also added that the strike was “not directed at a hospital” and caused no damage to the facility.

The Israeli military has often accused Hamas of embedding itself within civilian infrastructure, including hospitals. However, in 2024 the head of the international criminal court’s Palestine investigation said claims about the presence of Hamas fighters in Gaza’s hospitals had been “grossly exaggerated” .

Israel has killed Palestinian medical workers en masse since the start of the war in Gaza. According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, at least 1,700 have been killed by Israeli attacks. Rights groups say the Israeli military has engaged in systematic destruction of civilian infrastructure, including medical infrastructure.

The UN has repeatedly called on Israel to stop its restrictions on the entry of supplies to allow Palestinians to prepare for the winter and begin to rebuild the destroyed strip.

The result is a healthcare system “experiencing systemic collapse, severely undermining its capacity to meet the basic health needs of the civilian population”, according to a UN report in August.

The humanitarian situation is also deteriorating, as heavy rains exacerbate crowded and unsanitary living conditions, leading to the spread of infectious diseases.

Israel has continued to bomb Gaza on a near-daily basis despite a ceasefire signed in October 2025, killing at least 1,705 people since then. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of violating the understandings of the ceasefire.

The war began after a Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 that killed about 1,200 people.

More than 74,000 people have been killed and more than 175,000 injured in Israel’s war in Gaza. A UN independent international commission of inquiry found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court for war crimes. Israel denies these claims.

title: Victorian election 2026: Labor suffers historic defeat as Coalition wins majority government
author: Benita Kolovos and Henry Belot
text:
Jess Wilson to become state’s first popularly elected female premier as Ben Carroll loses seat in 2026 state election, and Greens and One Nation surge

Victoria election live results: votes tracker, map and seat counts

Live blog: Victorian election 2026 – latest news and results

Victorian Labor has suffered a historic defeat, ending 12 years of government, with the Coalition winning majority government and the Greens securing a record number of seats.

One Nation was on course to win more than 20% of the primary vote, but struggled to pick up lower house seats on a night when huge swings and three- or even four-party contests in many electorates made preference flows difficult to calculate.

At 36, Wilson will become Victoria’s youngest leader since federation and the first woman to be popularly elected as the state’s premier – a feat neither Jacinta Allan nor Joan Kirner achieved.

In her victory speech, Wilson spoke directly to Labor voters who had abandoned the party and said her team would “work every single day to demonstrate that you were right to place your trust in us”.

“I know that for many of you this is the first time that you have ever voted Liberal. And for others, it was the first time you have ever given us your preference.

“I realise that you have lent us your vote. We don’t own it.”

Carroll lost his seat of Niddrie in Melbourne’s north-western suburbs, which Labor had held for its entire 50 year history. It is the first time a Victorian premier has lost their seat at a state election.

In a speech to party faithful shortly after 8.30pm, Carroll took full responsibility for Labor’s crushing defeat.

“This is a significant loss for Labor,” Carroll said. “It’s not the result we wanted, but it is a result we accept.

“As leader of the party, I take full responsibility. Democracy is both beautiful and brutal. Beautiful, because we get to witness the will of the people. And brutal, because it is so difficult and painful to lose.

“But Victorians have spoken. And their message is clear. They want change.”

As of 10pm the Greens were on course to secure eight seats – holding Brunswick, Richmond and Melbourne and winning Pascoe Vale, Preston, Northcote and Footscray from Labor, and Prahran from the Liberals.

If voting trends from Saturday evening’s counting continued, it appeared possible the Greens might win more lower house seats than Labor, making it the official opposition.

The party’s state leader, Ellen Sandell, told ecstatic supporters the result was “not an overwhelming endorsement of the Liberals or One Nation”.

“This result is a rejection of the Labor party that has moved so far away from the values they once held, and it is a rejection of the old party politics that just is not working for people.

“We are sending more Greens to parliament than ever before at a time that could not be more crucial.

“When we say we have to replace the major parties, we are serious. It was always about more than just winning seats in Parliament. It was about building a movement and a progressive political force with the courage and the conviction to stand up for what it believes.”

One Nation secured more than 20% of the statewide primary vote – up from 0.22% in 2022 – but seemed likely to gain very few lower house seats. It appeared on course to win the regional district of Murray Plains, held by the Nationals, and was in contention in Sunbury on Melbourne’s north-western fringe, previously held by Labor.

At One Nation Victoria’s campaign event, it was the federal leader Pauline Hanson who addressed the party faithful. The state leader, Warren Pickering, failed to win the seat of Pakenham, which went to the Liberals.

Hanson congratulated Wilson and said she “had a big job ahead of her to clear up Labor’s mess”.

“For Victoria’s sake, I wish her and her team well,” Hanson said.

One Nation’s lower house prospects appear to have been hurt by a complex preference count in Labor-held seats it targeted. As Labor fell to third place in some seats, its preferences flowed to the Liberals.

Early in the night several former Labor seats were called for the Liberals, including Frankston and Mordialloc in the south-east, Hastings on the Mornington Peninsula and Box Hill and Ringwood, in the eastern suburbs. The seat of South Barwon also went to the Liberals, the first time the party has won the seat from Labor since the 1990s.

Point Cook, Sydenham, Werribee and Melton – traditional Labor strongholds in Labor’s west and north – also fell to the Liberals.

Labor MP Steve Dimopoulous, who is seen by some as a potential leader of the party if he holds on to his seat, offered a sincere apology to Labor faithful.

“This is an absolutely unequivocal report card on the Labor government,” Dimopoulous said.

The deputy Labor leader, Gabrielle Williams, another potential leadership candidate, said she was “deeply saddened” by the result and the party needed to learn from its mistakes.

“Clearly we have to be deeply humbled by the results and take the lessons from them,” Williams said.

Federal Labor sources quickly began to distance themselves from the state election result. One described the result as the “perfect storm-of-shit moment in Victoria” that would not be repeated federally.

“There are upsides federally to the Liberals being in power and cutting and privatising stuff, and One Nation’s bluster and hollowness getting tiring,” they said.

title: Argentina fails to block UK-led oil drilling off Falkland Islands
author: Press Association
text:
International tribunal rules there does not appear to be basis for believing Buenos Aires has jurisdiction on islands

Argentina’s attempt to block oil drilling off the Falkland Islands has been rejected by an international tribunal.

Buenos Aires had called for the international tribunal for the law of the sea (ITLOS) to order a halt to the Sea Lion project, as part of its claim to sovereignty over the Falklands.

But in a decision read out by ITLOS president, Maurice Kamga, on Saturday, the court rejected Argentina’s arguments, saying there did not appear to be any basis for believing it had jurisdiction as the tribunal is unable to rule on questions of sovereignty.

Kamga said 18 judges had voted to reject Argentina’s claims, while three had voted to uphold them.

At a hearing earlier this month, Argentina said drilling should not be allowed until the issue of sovereignty had been resolved and asked ITLOS to issue a temporary injunction until a full arbitration hearing could be held.

But the UK attorney general, Ellie Reeves, said such an order would have “devastating consequences” for the Falkland Islanders and prevent them from developing their natural resources “as they are entitled to do so, pursuant to their fundamental right to self-determination”.

The Sea Lion development is a joint venture in the South Atlantic Ocean between British and Israeli companies, and contains an estimated 1.7bn barrels of oil.

The Argentinian president, Javier Milei, previously described the companies’ activities as unlawful and launched economic sanctions on people and firms involved in oil exploration around the islands.

High-security prisoner used soap to escape despite being handcuffed and chained to officer
author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
text:
Exclusive: inmate from HMP Manchester now back in custody after 13 hours on the run

A prisoner from one of England and Wales’s most dysfunctional high-security jails is believed to have used soap to help escape from officers while visiting a hospital for treatment.

The 36-year-old detained at HMP Manchester managed to slip away despite being cuffed and chained to an officer, sources told the Guardian. He is believed to have lathered his metal cuff with liquid soap and slipped his hand out while being given privacy to use a bathroom.

After 13 hours of freedom and a short pursuit on foot, the offender was detained and arrested by Greater Manchester police officers.

The incident has sparked a formal inquiry by the Ministry of Justice, and comes amid an increase in escapes from jails in England and Wales.

This is the second time this year that a prisoner has escaped after attending a Manchester hospital.

Marwan Jumaa, a 20-year-old Sudanese national deemed to be a risk to himself and others, was serving an indefinite secure hospital sentence for attacking two women. He escaped after being transferred from his secure hospital facility to North Manchester hospital for medical treatment in July.

Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the prison officers’ union, the POA, demanded that more officers should escort offenders from category A and B prisons to hospitals.

“This incident highlights the risks that officers face when escorting prisoners to and from hospitals. There should be a minimum of three officers on every hospital appointment instead of two under current rules,” he said.

The number of prisoners escaping from custody has steadily increased over the past three years. In 2025-26, 14 people escaped from custody across England and Wales, compared with 12 the year before, and nine in 2023-24.

HMP Manchester, once known as Strangeways and which houses category A and B prisoners, has been said to have some of the worst conditions across the England and Wales estate.

The category B prisoner escaped on the evening of 20 November after two prison officers accompanied him to a local hospital.

According to prison escort regulations, category B prisoners must wear “double handcuffs” – where both wrists are restrained close to each other and a prisoner is cuffed to a member of staff.

Subject to risk assessment, the double cuff can be adjusted to a single cuff and a ratchet chain when privacy and hand movements are required, such as when using the toilet or shower. This allows the prison officers to give an offender privacy in a room or cubicle while still being attached to an officer via a chain, which can be more than a metre long.

Sources said that the prisoner had been placed in a single cuff and chain but had escaped from his cuff while using a bathroom. Police were alerted at 8.30pm and searched for the man overnight. He was located at 9.30am on Saturday, and was detained and arrested after attempting to flee on foot.

The internal MoJ investigation will focus on whether safety procedures were carried out at all times and if the man was handcuffed properly.

A spokesperson for Greater Manchester police said: “We received a call shortly before 8.30pm on Friday 20 November that a 36-year-old man had absconded from lawful custody whilst at hospital.

“Officers deployed and utilising specialist resources conducted a full search over the course of the evening and into the morning. The man was safely detained at around 9.30am on Saturday 21 November following a short foot chase and further arrested on suspicion of escaping lawful custody. He has been transported back to custody.”

Prison sources said the escape of a prisoner held in a high-security prison was still relatively rare.

In September 2023, Daniel Khalife, 23, sparked a high-profile search when he broke out of HMP Wandsworth by clinging to the underside of a food delivery truck. At the time he was being held on remand for spying charges.

Last year, an escaped prisoner tried to flee armed police by ramming them with his getaway car. Jay Bennett, 33, was serving a nine-year sentence when he absconded from HMP Sudbury in Derbyshire.

An official report into HMP Manchester conducted earlier this year by the prisons watchdog found large quantities of drugs flown in by drones, an obvious rat infestation and violence against prisoners and staff.

The report by Charlie Taylor, HM chief inspector of prisons, said the jail was “in a precarious state”. In 2024, he invoked an urgent notification, which automatically triggers ministers to intervene in the jail’s management.

A Prison Service spokesperson said: “This individual is now back in custody. We have launched an investigation into this incident and any prisoner who is unlawfully at large faces extra time in prison.”

title: Deal with Epstein lawyer and accountant could block victims’ other claims, experts warn
author: Victoria Bekiempis in New York
text:
Concern that settlement to resolve suit against pair may stymie legal claims that involve child sexual abuse material

As the clock ticks toward final settlement for a sex-trafficking-related lawsuit against Jeffrey Epstein ’s accountant and attorney, some experts are expressing concern that the agreement might stymie survivors’ search for justice in other litigation involving child sexual abuse images.

The suit involves Darren Indyke and Richard D Kahn, who for decades worked as Epstein’s personal lawyer and accountant respectively. Both men also serve as executors of Epstein’s estate. Indyke and Kahn have insisted they knew nothing about Epstein’s crimes and have rejected allegations of wrongdoing.

In the soon-to-be-settled 2024 Manhattan federal court civil complaint against them, survivors’ attorneys allege that Indyke and Kahn “were personally essential to the Epstein enterprise’s success – among other things, they helped structure Epstein’s bank accounts and cash withdrawals to give Epstein and his associates access to large amounts of cash in furtherance of sex trafficking”.

A final settlement hearing in this trafficking-related case is scheduled for 2 December, during which a judge might sign off on the agreement brokered between survivors’ attorneys at Boies Schiller & Flexner LLP, and Indyke and Kahn. This agreement would establish a $35m settlement pool for survivors who qualify for compensation with these claims, according to court papers.

Epstein, a high-powered financier who counted numerous wealthy and prominent men as his associates, was arrested in July 2019 and charged with sex-trafficking minors following years of allegations against him. The Manhattan US attorney’s office said that his victims were as young as age 14 when he abused them. He killed himself in jail while awaiting trial.

Jennifer Freeman of Marsh Law, who helms other litigation against Epstein, has voiced concerns about the proposed settlement, namely that this deal might set up roadblocks to legal claims against his estate that involve child sex abuse material, or CSAM.

Survivors and law enforcement have said that Epstein possessed, transported, produced and distributed CSAM over decades. Freeman said she fears that Epstein’s estate could try arguing that the proposed Kahn/Indyke settlement protects his estate from any possible litigation brought by CSAM survivors.

“We objected to the settlement on the grounds that CSAM has its own separate claim with its own statutory remedies and this was not, in our view, considered in putting together this settlement,” Freeman told the Guardian.

Freeman represents two women in a 15 September lawsuit involving CSAM claims, as well as several class members of the trafficking-related litigation.

“We fully support the existence of a settlement for survivors, and we want that to go forward, and we very much hope it does,” Freeman said. “However, we believe that the release of [Epstein’s] estate doesn’t make sense here, since the case was not against the estate – it was against two individuals, the lawyer and the accountant.”

Freeman also said she had concerns that survivors might not be aware of the proposed settlement and what she believes might be potential implications on CSAM claims against Epstein’s estate. Freeman wants any Epstein survivor who endured CSAM abuse – including those who participate in the trafficking settlement – to have an opportunity to pursue claims related directly to CSAM.

While the judge on 16 September extended the deadline for survivors to submit or opt out of trafficking-related claims, Freeman said that “we’ve heard from many, particularly those who are outside the United States, [who] had no idea anything was going on”.

“They don’t have class actions typically in their countries, so this would not be a familiar process for them to look out for or understand … that it might apply to them.”

CSAM claims “should not be included in the settlement at all. That should be explicit,” Freeman said of her hopes for the final agreement. “The release of the estate should be at least limited and, in my view, eliminated.”

Asked for comment, attorneys for Indyke and Kahn deferred to prior statements on allegations against them.

In a recent lawsuit against them brought by New Mexico’s attorney general, Raúl Torrez, one of their lawyers said they “emphatically rejected” claims “they were complicit in or in any way knowingly facilitated Mr Epstein’s sexual abuse or trafficking – conduct that by all accounts occurred behind closed doors, in secluded locations, and at times when neither Mr Indyke nor Mr Kahn was present.

“Not a single woman has ever accused Mr Indyke or Mr Kahn of committing sexual abuse or witnessing sexual abuse, nor claimed at any time that she or anyone else reported to them any allegation of Mr Epstein’s abuse,” the statement also said.

Attorneys for Indyke and Kahn do not agree with concerns that the trafficking-related settlement is over-broad. Daniel Ruzumna, who represents Indyke, said: “As the parties pointed out at the hearing and the court appeared to recognize, the putative class only includes women who were sexually abused and/or trafficked by Epstein.”

“That would include any woman who also may also have a CSAM-related claim, in which case that woman may be entitled to a larger recovery from the settlement fund,” Ruzumna said. “But if a woman only had CSAM-related claims, she would not be part of the class … at the September 16 2026 hearing, the parties made clear that women with CSAM-only claims (ie who were not abused or trafficked themselves) are not part of the class and therefore would not release claims.”…

title: US oligarchs enriched by ‘transactional’ Trump face fierce scrutiny in new Congress
author: Peter Stone in Washington
text:
Democrats pledge aggressive investigations into Trump-allied billionaires and how president’s policies have boosted their bottom lines

For an elite circle of Donald Trump billionaire allies who lavished tens of millions of dollars on his campaign, vanity projects and crypto ventures, his second administration has boosted their bottom lines through lax oversight, tax breaks, federal contracts and other perks.

But with Democrats winning control of Congress in the midterms, House and Senate investigations are being planned for 2027 into several Maga oligarchs in hi-tech and crypto industries, examining how their firms and the president benefited from his “transactional” governing style, according to Democratic lawmakers and scholars.

Trump allies expected to face scrutiny by congressional panels looking, in part, at how Trump’s pay-to-play modus operandi has financially and politically benefited them include Space X mogul Elon Musk, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, and crypto titans such as Binance founder Changpeng Zhao.

Trump’s own wealth soared by $2.7bn since he won the presidency again in 2024 – due in good measure to “crypto ventures and overseas deals”, according to a Forbes report in September.

Additionally, Trump’s sons, Eric and Donald Jr, have notched sizable financial gains in tech, crypto and other areas since Trump won again, and are expected to face Capitol Hill inquiries into ways their Oval Office ties may have benefited them.

White House and justice department lawyers in November sent threatening letters to key congressional Democrats, warning they could face scrutiny, and perhaps criminal charges, if they investigated some of Trump’s big-money patrons and their federal contracts.

Scholars and legal experts who have tracked some of Trump’s financial moves, boosting his personal fortune and increasing the wealth of his big patrons, see ample evidence that the ties between Trump and some of his leading donors and business allies have hurt American democracy.

“The personal wealth of Trump, his family, and those in his inner circle, as well as Trump’s vanity projects, are being funded by the very tech titans whose own wealth and power has been boosted by this administration’s policies and actions,” Cornell economist Eswar Prasad said in an email.

Prasad earlier this year raised red flags about Trump’s dealings with “crypto tycoons”, telling the Guardian: “Trump and his family have hardly been shy about cozying up to crypto tycoons, and have been quite brazen in their pay-for-play approach to this sector.”

While the Hill investigations are in planning stages, tech leaders led by Elon Musk have clearly been big winners in the second Trump administration .

Trump and Republicans forged especially close ties with Musk, the world’s richest man, who spent almost $300m in 2024 to help Trump win, and then about $450m in the midterms in mostly failed efforts to help GOP candidates.

According to an in-depth report this fall from the nonpartisan Democracy Defenders Fund, Musk firms secured $6bn in government contracts while he was leading Trump’s “Doge” drive to cut federal spending, and another $10bn in contracts since he left his post last year.

Moreover, the study found 25 federal agencies or departments have “taken actions benefiting or potentially benefiting his businesses”.

The DDF report – Trump and Musk, 17 Months Later – also found that Musk’s net worth “more than doubled since he left Doge in May 2025, growing from approximately $419bn to between $900bn and $1tn”.

“The central finding is that the current government ethics framework allows the world’s richest person – a major political donor and former government official – to earn billions from federal contracts while his companies receive favorable treatment across government,” the report concluded.

Before the elections, Musk on X vowed to hit back against those who go after him, writing : “Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them.”

Separately, Huang, who resigned as Nvidia CEO after reports of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy spurred fears of China gaining significant access to Nvidia’s valuable microchips, looks to have benefited from the president’s pay-to-play governing style.

In a stunning twist, 11 days after Huang quit, and facing clear pressure from Trump and others in his administration, Nvidia announced Huang would return as CEO, a move which fueled bipartisan concerns and calls for hearings next month.

Huang in 2025 was among the biggest known donors to Trump’s prized ballroom, reportedly giving $25m to finance the venture, according to Public Citizen, a liberal watchdog.

Moreover, Trump’s financial disclosures in 2026 revealed Nvidia stock trading over 100 times since he returned to office with a combined transaction value between 27m and 97m, according to Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (Crew).

Trump has said all his stocks are managed solely by independent outside advisers and he has no role in stock trading. Trump has also repeatedly denied any conflicts of interest or quid pro quos as president.

Trump and his billionaire commerce secretary Howard Lutnick reportedly ignored national security intelligence warnings and allowed Nvidia to sell its advanced chips to the Singapore-based datacenter firm Megaspeed, which was until August 2025 run by Alice Huang, the alleged spy who had an affair with Jensen Huang.

According to press reports, Alice Huang was in touch with China’s spy agency for months when her firm sold some of Nvidia’s advanced chips to other datacenters in south-east Asia with China ties, and some of which were suspected of being smuggled to China, fueling bipartisan criticism and some internal administration dissent.…

title: ‘Please can I have one more picture’: the US airmen accused of child sexual abuse in UK who avoided British trial
author: Rob Evans, Harry Davies, Louisa Loveluck and Emine Sinmaz
text:
Guardian investigation reveals US military personnel, including ‘multi-child molester’, convicted in courts martial

When Jacob Ozbirn, an American airman, drove to a country lane near a Derbyshire hotel one summer’s evening, he was expecting to meet a 12-year-old girl he had been grooming for sex.

In the previous days, he had sent explicit messages to her and two other girls, encouraging them to send him naked photos, despite having been told by all three that they were aged 12 or 13.

In one message, he wrote: “There is nothing to be afraid of. I will take care of you! And please can I have one more picture.”

Ozbirn drove two hours from RAF Mildenhall, the huge US airbase in Suffolk where he was stationed, to meet one of them near Burton upon Trent. But he had walked into a sting run by “paedophile hunters”, members of the public who pose online as girls to lure suspected paedophiles to meetings where they confront them.

Ozbirn told the paedophile hunters he was simply seeking to educate the girls about dangerous predators, but they notified Derbyshire police who detained him.

Ozbirn should have been investigated by the local police force and, if necessary, prosecuted in a British criminal court. Instead, Derbyshire police handed over the investigation to the US military police. He was brought before a court martial, held on the Mildenhall base, and sent to a US military jail for three years.

The Guardian has now identified at least 21 American airmen in the UK who have been convicted of child sexual abuse offences in the last decade. Only three were prosecuted in UK courts.

The rest were brought in front of US courts martial, which, critics argue, provide a more limited form of justice. Juries, sometimes all-male, are made up of the defendant’s peers. Unlike hearing in the open British courts, members of the public are unable to easily attend courts martial held on US airbases.

Accounts of these proceedings are often too sparse to determine whether UK police have, or should have, been involved.

Documents relating to courts martial are published on a public register in an inconsistent way, often disappearing with no explanation. Charges are described in a limited way or not at all.

Rachel VanLandingham , a retired lieutenant colonel and former military lawyer, said that for decades the transparency of the US military justice system had been “woefully inadequate”. “It’s been brought to the military’s attention time after time again,” she said. “It’s intentionally opaque. They want it to be opaque.”

There are more than 12,000 US military personnel working on at least 15 bases and facilities across the UK. Under an official agreement dating back to the 1950s , any US military personnel accused of breaking the law should be investigated by a British police force unless the alleged offences are committed while on duty or against another member of the US armed forces, its property, or a dependant such as a spouse or child.

But the Guardian has uncovered a growing number of cases in which UK police forces have acquiesced to requests by the US military to take control of investigations into potential wrongdoing by members of the American armed forces.

The agreement is now the subject of a high-level internal inquiry examining whether US military personnel stationed in Britain are being prosecuted properly.

The inquiry, which involves at least four Whitehall departments and police chiefs, was set up after the Guardian revealed in June how UK police had permitted the US military to take over an investigation into an American pilot who strangled a British woman in his flat in Cambridge.

The pilot, Jacob Wulfson, was instead tried in a US court martial that was held on his base at RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk . Downing Street said it was “deeply distressing” and “very concerning” that the UK authorities were not involved in prosecuting Wulfson.

The US military uses courts martial to prosecute its personnel for a range of types of offences such as sexual violence against women, assaults, drug-taking and failing to obey orders.

An analysis shows that out of the 63 military personnel who have been convicted at courts martial in the UK going back to 2016, 18 have been convicted of child sexual abuse offences – more than a quarter of the total.

The offences include the rape and sexual abuse of children under the age of 12 and acquiring large amounts of child pornography.

Most recently, two airmen were convicted in October in separate courts martial that took place on the Lakenheath base.

The first airman was sentenced to 10 years in a military jail for sexually abusing a child and possessing and obtaining child pornography. He is known only as Lucero, as the US military has not published his first name.

William Berroa was sent to a military jail for two years for possessing and viewing child abuse images. The US air force has published no details of their offending.

The Guardian asked the US air force military police, the Office of Special Investigations (OSI), if it had asked the British police to take over jurisdiction for the investigation of these cases.

The OSI did not answer this question. In a statement, it said: “As in all our investigations, the Air Force Office of Special Investigations worked with our UK partners to determine investigative primacy.

“Extensive negotiations took place to establish jurisdiction. While we cannot give details, these were decisions that were not made quickly or spuriously. Ultimately, the local authorities have the right of first refusal on all investigative matters.”

The US military wants to handle as many of the prosecutions of its personnel as possible . The Americans frequently ask to take over investigations from UK police forces, even when it appears clear that they would fall within the responsibility of the British authorities. Many times the UK police agree. But sometimes they refuse.…

Drones ‘swarmed’ US army base at RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk in November
author: Harry Taylor
text:
Personnel told to take cover after ‘suspected unauthorised activity’ of six drones that were repelled but not recovered

Drones reportedly swarmed a US army base in Suffolk earlier this month and were not recovered after being repelled.

Personnel at RAF Lakenheath were told to take cover on 13 November after “suspected unauthorised drone activity”. The US air force confirmed the so-called Charlie alert at the time, the second-highest threat level, but released few details. Sirens could be heard at the base . Iran is suspected of being involved.

However, the Financial Times has now reported about six drones were seen flying around the base. RAF Lakenheath has been home to the USAF since 1948, with the US taking control in 1950.

The 48th Fighter Wing, the largest US fighter jet operation in Europe, is based there. About 7,000 personnel are on site. US counter-drone technology was used to stop the drones, but they were not recovered by British or US personnel, the newspaper reported. The US has refused to say what systems were deployed.

There are fears that the UK and US cannot rule out whether the drones were armed, or had spying equipment attached. The USAF urged personnel to be vigilant and report suspicious activity.

A spokesperson said: “For operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection measures or [counter drone] systems in place at any given location; however, we want to make clear that our security forces, in cooperation with our host nation partners, take a proactive integrated and layered approach to base defence and are ready to address potential threats.

“We continue to work very closely with our UK partners to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, US and host nation civilians, contractors, families and greater communities. We encourage everyone in our communities to remain vigilant and report any suspicious activity immediately to local authorities.”

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “The protection of our bases is a top priority, and we continually review and strengthen our security arrangements.

“Ministry of Defence police and Suffolk police worked closely with USAF Security Forces to respond to reports of unauthorised drone activity at RAF Lakenheath on 13 November, and the situation was quickly resolved, with RAF Lakenheath returning to normal security and force protection measures.”

The incident came almost two years after a number of drones were spotted near RAF Lakenheath, as well as neighbouring RAF Mildenhall and RAF Feltwell, which is also used by the USAF.

In November 2024, it confirmed “small unmanned aerial systems” were seen over a two-day period that month. The USAF said it was unclear whether the drones were hostile. British forces were deployed to help defend the base.

Lakenheath was built during the second world war as a decoy airfield, before being converted and playing a role in bombing raids on Europe. The US arrived after the end of the conflict.

With the onset of the cold war, the US stationed nuclear-armed B-29 Superfortress bombers at the base in case of attack by the Soviet Union.

Earlier this year, a security alert was sparked when a suspected terror plot was uncovered near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, and an alleged trespass incident took place at RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire.

The incident at Fairford led to a major incident being declared. It led to dozens of residents being evacuated, and a large cordon was put in place. Both bases are used by the US.

Two men have been charged with the incident at Fairford in September. They will stand trial at Woolwich crown court next year. Separately, two men were arrested in connection with alleged trespass at Molesworth.

The US has since removed planes from Mildenhall and Fairford in response to the perceived threat from Iran. Last month, the UK’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, along with 35 allies, signed a statement condemning the threat posed by Iran to the UK and its allies.

Miliband also summoned the Iranian ambassador as he issued a statement which said: “Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil.”

Stephen Doughty, minister of state for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, later said Iran posed a “significant threat” to UK both directly and through its proxies.

title: Spain to vote in election that could put far right in power for first time since Franco
author: Sam Jones in Madrid
text:
Socialist PM Pedro Sánchez’s high-stakes gamble could end in defeat to a coalition including the far-right Vox

Spaniards head to the polls on Sunday to vote in a high-stakes snap general election that could put a far-right party in government for the first time since the country’s return to democracy after the death of Gen Francisco Franco in 1975.

Although the next election was not due until summer next year, Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, called the vote in October after three rightwing and far-right parties voted down the emergency legislation that his government had proposed to address the country’s housing crisis .

Huge public anger over soaring rents exploded in September after the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal , an 87-year-old woman who was removed from her home in Madrid because she could not afford the 230% rent increase demanded by the investment fund that had bought her apartment.

Faced with nationwide protests, Sánchez’s coalition minority government put together a package of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.

Sánchez opted for one of his characteristic gambles and announced the early election after the proposals were torpedoed by the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox and the rightwing Catalan separatist Junts.

The prime minister – an inveterate risk-taker whose penchant for unpredictable moves has fuelled his political survival – calculated that his opponents’ decision to block the housing overhauls could work in his electoral favour.

On Friday morning, Sánchez said he was confident of victory. “I can’t conceive of us losing,” he told Cadena Ser radio , adding: “When progressive Spain gets going, it’s unstoppable.”

But while his Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) has managed to narrow the distance between it and the PP, which is leading the polls, to fewer than three percentage points, the right looks likely to form the next government in coalition with the far right.

Survey after survey predicts the PP will finish first but fall short of a majority, leaving it dependent on a deal with Vox. Between them, the two parties are forecast to secure a joint majority well above the 176 required seats in Spain’s 350-seat congress of deputies. Even if the PSOE enjoys a last-minute surge and comes first, the parliamentary arithmetic suggests it would struggle to cobble together another coalition administration with the support of its allies in the leftwing Broad Front alliance and with that of regional nationalist parties.

Choosing housing as a key battleground allowed Sánchez to attempt to shift the focus away from the corruption allegations facing his inner circle. It also offered him the chance to move on from his government’s much-criticised handling of the crisis in Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta , which was sparked when about 80,000 people crossed into the territory from neighbouring Morocco in the space of 48 hours.

But some of the energy of the government’s resurgent campaign was sapped at the end of October when 69 people were killed in Spain’s second deadly rail crash in just nine months .

The PP and Vox have used the two crashes to accuse the government of failing in its basic duty to keep Spaniards safe. More broadly, the PP and Vox are using the poll as a referendum on what they disdainfully refer to as “ sanchismo ”. They argue that the style of government favoured by the prime minister and his allies is cynical, corrupt, opportunistic and self-serving.

“Spain deserves a decent prime minister and [Sánchez] isn’t one,” the PP leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, told viewers during a head-to-head debate between the two men last week.

Sánchez, however, insisted that while he had made errors, Spain was in a better state than it was when he came to office in 2018. “My government hasn’t been perfect; I’ve made mistakes,” he said. “But I’m also fully aware that we have always governed in the right direction.”

The prime minister has also sought to depict the snap election as a stark choice between progressive forces and reactionary ones – as typified by the PP’s putative alliance with Vox.

“You must decide whether you want our country to move backwards or continue moving forwards, and whether you prefer a government that works for the interests of the majority of society,” he told Spaniards as he announced the vote.

Over recent days, the government has tried to underline its commitment to social justice and equality by proposing a new tax on fortunes of more than €100m (£84m) that would help fund childcare, housing and public services.

The PP, meanwhile, is promising to lower taxes, build 1m homes, and “restore the country’s ambition and self-esteem”. Vox’s manifesto , which includes plans to have Sánchez and his government prosecuted “for treason and crimes against the security of the state” over the Ceuta mass crossing, focuses on deregulation, “remigration” and giving Spanish-born people priority over those born abroad for housing and public services.

Although the PP’s previous leader, Pablo Casado, famously repudiated Vox and its ideology, accusing the party of practising a politics based on “fear, anger, resentment and revenge” , the PP has repeatedly entered into regional coalition governments with Vox and now runs four of Spain’s autonomous regions with the party.

In recent days, the PP and Vox have attempted to call into question the fairness and transparency of the election, making baseless claims that the government may seek to rig postal votes. Vox’s leader, Santiago Abascal, has also suggested, without providing evidence, that Sánchez is working to undermine democracy and change the country’s demographic makeup .

title: Under the influence: how creator marketing upended advertising
author: Mark Sweney
text:
Brands are piggybacking off the potential sales that targeting millions of ardent followers can bring – but there are risks

F rom the Avon ladies to the former Sex Pistols lead singer John Lydon selling butter , personal endorsement of products is a well-trodden form of marketing with significant gains – and pitfalls. More recently, the practice of teaming up with social media influencers has become a boom in the ad industry over the last decade – and came firmly into the spotlight this week.

First, the Guardian revealed that Unilever, the consumer goods behemoth behind huge brands including Dove soap to Hellmann’s mayonnaise, had slashed its almost £100m TV ad budget and was ploughing funds into online influencer marketing instead.

Then, a furore broke out over Andy Burnham’s interview with a TikToker, which involved filming a parody of Hugh Grant’s famous Love Actually dance inside 10 Downing Street.

The attempt to burnish Brand Burnham was further tarnished when it emerged that two more influencers, who had been invited to events at the prime minister’s residence, had posted clips filmed on the steps of No 10 featuring lewd, explicit or inappropriate lyrics .

The incident reignited the debate about the risks of tapping the “wild west” of online influencers and content creators in order to reach younger audiences increasingly trading TV for social media channels.

Burnham has said he will not apologise for his headlong rush to embrace influencers to reach young audiences – a government spokesperson meekly explained that content creators are “obviously responsible” for what they post – but the fallout is a stark reminder of the potential problems.

Nevertheless, brands big and small are piggybacking off the potential sales that can be drummed up by targeting the millions of ardent fans of influencers.

By the end of the decade more than $9bn (£6.9bn) will be spent on the so-called creator economy, more than brands will spend on running ads on traditional TV and streaming services, according to the consultancy Madison and Wall.

“The oldest marketing strategy of all time is human advocacy and recommendation,” says Jessica Tamsedge, the chief executive of the ad agency Dentsu Creative UK and Ireland. “Whether it is the Avon lady or celebrity endorsement … now it is about the different types of voices that are enlisted to do different jobs for businesses and brands. However, that doesn’t mean using them is automatically good marketing.

“When you go into a creator-led strategy there is enormous variation between successful and unsuccessful campaigns.”

Earlier this month, Space NK faced a consumer backlash for organising a trip for celebrities and influencers, including Stacey Solomon and Alison Hammond, to the five-star country house hotel in Surrey to launch the beauty product retailer’s festive range.

Consumers criticised the luxury staycation – which included beauty treatments, hair and makeup by brands including YSL and GHD and a lavish Christmas party – as being “tone deaf” given the pressure on consumers’ finances, particularly as the festive period piles pressure on budgets.

Nevertheless, it can be argued that the risk of getting it wrong can potentially be far outweighed by the reward of getting right.

In May, Kathryn Turner, the director of product development at M&S Food, started posting on her own TikTok with about 30 followers and a couple of young staff supporting her.

She has quickly become a viral sensation - Marks & Spencer’s gen-Z marketing dream – with about 700,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram.

A video released this month in which Turner championed a new chocolate and cornflake cookie, prompted long queues and Covid-style scenes of panic buying as people rushed to bakery counters at some M&S stores.

Meanwhile, Unilever said this week it had upped its network of influencers and creators to more than 500,000, an almost seven-fold increase in two years.

When Fernando Fernandez took over as chief executive in March last year he said he wanted “an influencer in every zip code in the globe”, a strategy that has completely upended how the Anglo-Dutch company spends its €8bn (£6.7bn) annual marketing budget.

In the UK, where Unilever has historically been a top-three TV advertiser, it has more than halved its budget, including almost completely disappearing from Channel 4 , one of the country’s biggest broadcasters. Unilever’s partners have included the former Love Island contestant Molly-Mae Hague on laundry detergent and fabric conditioner brands and the beauty creator Jen Chae.

Understandably, the TV industry is up in arms about the idea that running ads in The Great British Bake Off and I’m A Celebrity… Get Me Out Of Here! may no longer be the best use of marketing spend.

“TV advertising is the decision that makes other marketing decisions better,” says Lindsey Clay, the chief executive of Thinkbox, the marketing body for commercial TV in the UK. “Advertisers shouldn’t sacrifice what works hardest for what feels newest. Not every advertiser is following the evidence.

“If they were, TV would be the last place they’d cut to fund influencers. Influencers clearly have their place, but shifting money from TV to fund them is self-defeating.”

Despite the occasional misfire, the influencer and creator market has rapidly matured, according to the Influencer Marketing Trade Body (IMTB), which was set up to professionalise the industry in 2021. That was the year that the UK ad watchdog “named and shamed” reality TV stars for repeatedly failing to tell followers when they were paid to promote products in posts.…

title: DWP cyber incident ‘probably an attack’, says former UK chief technology officer
author: Kevin Rawlinson
text:
Government took down pensions and benefits portal on Thursday but said regular payments will not be affected

A serious cyber incident that forced ministers to take down online benefits and pension services was “probably an attack”, the UK’s former chief technology officer has said.

The Department for Work and Pensions took down several systems that appeared to still be offline on Saturday morning. David Knott, who led government technology until December 2025, said much infrastructure was outdated, and underinvestment in defence and increasing sophistication of attacks meant it was only getting more vulnerable.

“The government has been very sensible in using quite precise language, and being very evidence-based in the way they’ve reported it,” he told BBC Newsnight on Friday evening. “At the same time, some of that language does tell me it’s probably an attack.

“They’ve used the word ‘cyber’, which normally means it’s an attack. They’ve taken down some of the citizen-facing services, which implies to me that there’s some kind of attack could be mounted through the front door. So my strong suspicion is this is an attack.”

Downing Street said there was no evidence a “malicious actor” had targeted other departments. The government took its benefits portal down late on Thursday after detecting “unusual activity” – meaning people were unable to check their state pension, make a disability benefits application or claim universal credit.

The DWP makes about 2.5m regular payments a day, and it is understood that reported delays are not related to the cyber incident. The department urged people to be alert to any scams related to the outage and stressed that the government would never ask people to confirm bank details or click a link.

DWP insiders said payments for Friday would already have been sent earlier in the week, but there could be a backlog of manual payments running into tens of thousands due early next week to be processed over the weekend. Internal DWP systems were restored on Friday, allowing officials to begin working again, but the public-facing portal remained offline.

It also said people should contact their benefit helpline if they were having urgent difficulties and confirmed that no one would face a sanction for not meeting conditions while the system was offline.

Knott told Newsnight government systems were under attack every second of every day, saying: “There’s a statistic that, if you put an unprotected PC on the internet, it will get attacked within 27 seconds. And that’s a PC with no interesting assets on it. If you imagine, if you were holding the country’s tax records or health records or pension records, then you’re under attack all the time.”

He added: “The challenges in defending against cyber-attacks has been an asymmetric conflict for quite a long time; it’s really hard to defend, and it’s getting easier and easier and easier to attack. A lot of people are using AI tools to mount those attacks, which just makes it easier and easier to do. At the same time, if you’ve got systems that haven’t been upgraded for several years, and they’ve got known security vulnerabilities in them, you don’t need an advanced AI model to figure out how to attack them.”

Knott said the government measured how much of its infrastructure would be considered out of date. “I think in 2023, it was 26%. In 2024, it was 28%. So the numbers were going in the wrong direction.”

A DWP spokesperson said: “We have taken some DWP services offline as a precaution following a cyber incident. We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible to minimise any disruption.

“Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal. Anyone experiencing delays or other issues with payments should call our helplines in the usual way. As we work to safely get our services back online, customers directly affected by this incident will not face sanctions.”

No 10 said work was being carried out “as quickly as possible” to restore services. Internal DWP systems were restored on Friday, allowing officials to begin working again, but the public-facing portal remained offline.

GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre and government experts are investigating the suspected hack. The UK’s data protection watchdog said it is in contact with the DWP about the incident.

title: Bezzecchi on pole, Marquez claims MotoGP qualifying title
author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
text:
Aprilia MotoGP rider Marco Bezzecchi took a commanding pole position for the season finale in Valencia, but the retiring Marc Marquez took the 2026 qualifying title. MotoGP's qualifying championship BMW M Award scores riders by qualifying position using the same top-15 points system as for grand prix finishes, and awards a BMW car to the winner each year.

Marquez was the winner seven consecutive times between 2013 and 2019, and then prevailed in 2025 before doubling up in what has now turned out to be his final season.

Bezzecchi was the only rival who had a shot at denying him a ninth Award in the final round, but second place for Marquez was enough to keep him ahead in the standings - despite the gargantuan 0.463s gap between them.

This came as Bezzecchi obliterated the MotoGP lap record at the track with a searing 1m27.844s.

Raul Fernandez used three soft rear tyres in Q2 and briefly sat on provisional pole but ultimately ended up nearly six tenths behind Bezzecchi in third.

Alex Marquez, Jorge Martin and Fabio Di Giannantonio made it a top six made up entirely of Aprilia and Ducati riders.

Pedro Acosta was third of three KTM riders in Q2, beaten by Enea Bastianini (seventh), stand-in Pol Espargaro (eighth) and also potential 2027 Ducati team-mate Fermin Aldeguer (ninth).

This was despite Espargaro crashing at Turn 1 late on shortly after setting his fastest lap (which he'd spent half of in Acosta's tow).

Ai Ogura, who tumbled at Turn 11 at the end, and Joan Mir completed the Q2 order.

Brad Binder was 0.029s away from a farewell Q2 appearance, losing out to Mir for the final Q1 transfer spot and settling for 13th on the grid - which means team-mate Acosta has maintained a perfect qualifying record versus his team-mates over the first three seasons of his MotoGP career.

Ducati factory stand-in Iker Lecuona was 14th, just half a tenth off Q2, while Johann Zarco was likewise close in 15th - and compatriot Fabio Quartararo led the Yamaha contingent one spot lower.

Wout van Aert to make cyclo-cross return in Antwerp, with World Championships tilt on the cards
author: Katy Madgwick
text:
Wout van Aert has confirmed his return to the cyclo-cross field for the 2026-2027 season, with the likely aim of representing Belgium at the UCI World Championships in Ostend in January.

According to Flemish newspaper , the Visma-Lease a Bike rider will make his debut on December 19 in Antwerp, the same place where he began his campaign last season, finishing 7th on the day.

Van Aert raced a reduced calendar of six races in 2025-2026 and, despite two second-place finishes, was unable to record a win in the discipline for the first time since his debut season in 2010. He was set to race eight races in total but an ankle fracture sustained in Mol in early January forced an early end to his winter programme.

This season he looks set to expand his off-road schedule, with the suggestion that he may race around 12 races, with the first indication that these will include the World Championships in Ostend on January 31, 2027, an outcome which Belgian national coach Angelo De Clercq had previously suggested was uncertain.

It's still a relatively late start for Van Aert, as hopes for a potential debut at the Superprestige series in Ruddervoorde were quashed by confirmation that the Belgian would attend Visma-Lease a Bike's Spanish training camp in early December.

While his exact race programme is yet to be determined, it looks increasingly likely that Van Aert will take aim at the world title in January. He had already confirmed he would opt out of the most recent edition in Hulst in 2026 prior to his ankle injury, moving on from the mud to targets on the road, with the Spring Classics his first major goals of the season.

This season could mark a return to Worlds for a tilt at a rainbow jersey that he won three years in a row, from 2016-2018. His three most recent attempts to repeat the feat have resulted in second-place finishes to his long-time rival, Mathieu van der Poel, including in Ostend in 2021. It's currently unclear whether or not the Dutchman intends to race off-road this winter.

As for Van Aert, the 32-year-old has reduced his participation in the off-road discipline where he made his name in recent seasons; however, he continues to include cyclocross as part of his schedule, racing every season since his junior debut in 2010. This season marks his 17th consecutive winter as an elite cyclo-cross rider.

title: Man Utd trigger Fernandes' one-year contract extension
text:
Manchester United have triggered their one-year option on captain Bruno Fernandes' contract.

The 32-year-old's deal was due to expire next summer but sources say both parties decided it was in their best interests to activate the option through to 2028.

It means overseas clubs will not be able to approach Fernandes when the transfer window opens on 1 January.

The Portugal international confirmed on Tuesday that discussions over a new contract had been paused. Sources say they will resume once United's league position has improved.

Fernandes has made 343 appearances for United, scoring 115 goals, since his £47m move from Sporting in January 2020.

Last season he broke the Premier League assists record and scooped all of the individual player of the year awards after an outstanding campaign as United finished third.

While there is doubt over his long-term future, extending the contract means United would be able to command a fee for Fernandes should he leave in the summer.

United had been open to selling Fernandes in the summer of 2025, with Saudi Pro-League club Al Hilal offering a huge deal.

After discussing the situation with his wife, Fernandes decided to stay, though he later said it "hurt" United were willing to sell him. He reiterated on Tuesday he was still ambitious to win the biggest honours in the game.

Fernandes is a doubt for Saturday's Premier League encounter with Brentford after returning from the Champions League trip to Sporting with a virus.

The playmaker, who scored both goals in the 2-2 draw with his former club, but did not train on Friday and head coach Mauricio Pochettino said he would take a decision on his captain's fitness on Saturday morning.

"We are going to assess during the day and then tomorrow see how he is when he wakes up," said Pochettino. "We are not going to take any risks."

Pochettino was criticised by former Liverpool and England midfielder Jamie Redknapp on the Overlap earlier this week.

Reference was made to the former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea coach high-fiving Sky Sports reporter Patrick Davidson after his side's 4-0 defeat at Liverpool on Sunday, as evidence Pochettino had lost his edge.

"When I saw Pochettino at Southampton and I saw him at Tottenham, he looked like he had that Argentinian dog in him," said Redknapp.

"I look at him now and he's high-fiving everyone, he's got the bracelets on, he's got the barnet. I think he's gone too nice."

It seems someone had mentioned the observation to Pochettino as he went off on a tangent at his Friday news conference when asked about a "crazy" first week that included red cards, refereeing errors, disallowed goals and a drone filming training.

"What are we going to do? Start to cry?" he asked. "No. We have to be strong, believe and keep going. I cannot judge the past. Who am I to do that? I was in Cincinnati. I was outside. I need to shut my mouth, say nothing and start from now.

"Sometimes we are so confusing two words that means something similar; nice and good. I am not nice. We have to be good. It is a different thing. We know when we need to push, when we need to be strong, and when we need to build something to improve the atmosphere and relationship and everything.

Pochettino also confirmed £70m midfielder Carlos Baleba is expected to be out until the last week in January with the hamstring injury he sustained against Roma on 3 November.

Forward Marcus Rashford had begun to do individual work outside as he tries to recover from a hip problem that has kept him out since 13 October.

title: The hill I will die on: Cheques are still the best way to pay for things | Claire Jackson
author: Claire Jackson
text:
A debit card might be quicker and easier, but there are thrills big and small to be had from whipping out your chequebook

I t often takes other people to identify your quirks. Mine is writing cheques, a fact I was made aware of recently by a younger colleague, who watched with bemusement as I filled one out. He’d never seen a chequebook in the wild, he explained, with the air of a naturalist encountering a rare species. He looked on as I, a millennial, wrote “one hundred and forty-one pounds and thirty pence only”, that last word thrilling in its assertiveness – I will pay my bill, South East Water, and not a penny more!

Having examined the whole procedure, including my procuring a stamp and envelope to send it off, he concluded – as so many have – that the process would be far better executed online. A friend also politely fed back that, although she appreciates how I “enclose a cheque” in every birthday card to her daughter, could I perhaps just do a bank transfer like everyone else?

While many aspects of the 1990s have resurfaced – baggy jeans, Nirvana T-shirts and casual sexism – the cheque is viewed with the same disdain as dial-up internet. But I maintain that, if you must pay for something, it is truly the ideal way.

First, scribbling – holding a pen or pencil and feeling it move across the page – is enjoyable. Paying via cheque thus becomes a simple pleasure – selecting the correct ink (anything other than blue or black is frowned upon; graphite is completely unacceptable), and signing with a writing instrument rather than a finger.

Financial transactions can also be hasty – something I realised after finding myself in debt. While I now (grudgingly) have a contactless card, I still fear I might tap without checking the amount and lose a fortune. That would never happen with a cheque.

Inherent trust is required in accepting a cheque, which adds to its affability. One of my favourite pubs, The Harrow Inn in Steep, Hampshire , politely warns: “We do not take credit or debit cards. Cash and cheques are welcome.” I discovered this on a day I had neither, and the owner happily served me lunch on the understanding that a cheque would be sent in the post forthwith (it was). Even when such goodwill is manipulated, the act is described with characteristically charming language – case in point, cheques “bouncing”.

Of course, there are benefits to digital banking, some of them unexpected. A friend’s young son has a Monzo account for his pocket money. Having ushered him away from the sweets being sold onboard as they were disembarking a Thames Clipper, she became occupied with her other child. When she looked up, her son had disappeared. Just as the boat slipped its moorings, her phone buzzed with a Monzo update that her son had just bought the contraband snacks – realising where he had gone, her family was swiftly united.

But this lady’s not for turning. I recently got a letter from HMRC informing me that I had overpaid my tax, and outlining the ways in which I might receive my refund. I don’t think I need to tell you which option I selected.

Claire Jackson is a journalist who writes about classical music, art and animals

title: Woman ‘traumatised’ by Sainsbury’s shoplifting ban after staff facial recognition error
author: Jessica Murray and Rosie Peters-McDonald
text:
Monia Indge, 58, who has terminal cancer, escorted from supermarket after staff using FaceWatch technology misidentified her

A woman with terminal cancer has been left “traumatised and violated” after being falsely accused of shoplifting and banned from Sainsbury’s by staff using facial recognition technology.

Monia Indge, 58, was shopping with her husband in the Walters Yard branch of Sainsbury’s in Bromley on 7 November when she was suddenly told to leave by a member of staff who told her she was “banned for life” from the store.

She said she was escorted from the shop by several security guards, but was given no answer when she asked what she had done wrong.

“I was so shocked, and being surrounded by security guards in that way was scary,” she said. “I used to be a teacher, and if any of the parents or children saw me, when I used to teach my students not to not steal … I thought my reputation was ruined.”

Indge was told to scan a QR code on a poster in the shop window, which directed her to the website for FaceWatch, a facial recognition security system used by more than 125 retailers across the UK, and being rolled out in 200 Sainsbury’s stores this year.

She spent several days desperately seeking answers from FaceWatch and Sainsbury’s. Ten days later, the supermarket responded with an apology, explaining that it had been a human error and offering a £150 voucher.

“My life is short as it is. To have to spend this time trying to clear my name, it’s horrendous,” she said. “The anxiety has been unbearable. I can’t sleep. I would not steal from anyone, and to be accused in front of everyone and escorted out with no reason is horrible.

“They view this as a glitch. I am not a glitch, I am a human being.”

Indge is the latest in a string of people who have been misidentified and asked to leave shops that use FaceWatch technology , and the case highlights growing concerns about retail staff being tasked with verifying real-time facial recognition alerts.

Large high-street chains including Sainsbury’s, B&M, Sports Direct and Home Bargains are all using FaceWatch to clamp down on rising rates of shop theft and antisocial behaviour.

The software scans the faces of shoppers in store and compares them against a database of people who have allegedly committed such offences previously. In Indge’s case, a member of staff mistook her for someone else who had been flagged in a FaceWatch alert.

The same thing happened to Oleh Sinkevych, 44, when he walked into his local Sainsbury’s branch in Canada Water to buy groceries on 24 October and was asked to leave by two members of staff.

“I started asking them, well, what happened? What did I do? What’s going on?” he said. “But they refused to talk to me.”

The email Sinkevych received from Sainsbury’s, apologising for the incident, explaining it was a manager’s mistake and offering him a £150 voucher, was identical to the one received by Indge a month later.

“It’s truly awful that your staff have to deal with aggression and theft,” Sinkevych responded. “I imagine the only thing worse is innocent people being wrongly accused of being aggressors or thieves. I’m not interested in any vouchers or certificates, but thank you for the kind offer.”

He has also complained to the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), saying whether or not the technology itself had failed, the system was “fundamentally broken” and the software was leading staff to “switch off their own judgement”.

Jack Coulson, the head of advocacy at Big Brother Watch, said the use of live facial recognition had turned shop workers into “untrained police officers” and he urged the ICO to take action.

The watchdog is advising the government on new biometrics laws and sets out guidelines on how companies should use facial recognition technology, but campaigners say it should be doing more to protect consumers.

Last month, Big Brother Watch organised a summit in parliament for people to share their experiences of being misidentified by facial recognition software – Sainsbury’s and FaceWatch were invited to represent their views, but neither attended.

Allison Gardner, the Labour MP for Stoke-on-Trent, chaired the event and said she was shocked by the stories she had heard. “Nobody really understands where liability lies,” she said. “I just want to get hold of that whole system and tear it apart.”

A Sainsbury’s spokesperson said: “We have sincerely apologised to Mr Sinkevych and Mrs Indge for their experiences in our stores and understand the significant upset these situations have caused, especially at such a difficult time for Mrs Indge and her family.

“Facial recognition technology has been introduced to help keep colleagues and customers safe amid unacceptably high levels of retail crime and it has been hugely successful, with eight in ten people added to the system not returning to reoffend.

“Our colleagues do an exceptional job every day in dealing with difficult situations professionally and helping to keep everyone safe but on the rare occasions we do see an error we provide training and support to prevent further incidents.”

A Facewatch spokesperson said: “We are very sorry for any distress these customers experienced, and we are particularly saddened to hear of Mrs Indge’s experience given her personal circumstances.

“In both cases the system correctly flagged the individuals it was looking for, but the human check before anyone acts on an alert is an important safeguard in the process, and we share responsibility for making sure it works every time.

“We are working closely with the Sainsbury’s team to support the managers using the system and to identify any further training or support they need.”

A spokesperson for the ICO said: “Facial recognition technology can help retailers detect and prevent crime and has clear benefits in the public interest.…

title: Pedrosa leaves KTM MotoGP project

KTM's long-serving test rider Dani Pedrosa has exited his role.

The now-41-year-old had joined KTM back in 2018 at the conclusion of his storied career in full-time grand prix racing competition.

He was a marquee signing for KTM, well-regarded for his feedback and feel but also specifically in being lured away from arch-rival manufacturer Honda.

Some notably competitive wildcard outings followed for Pedrosa on the KTM, and he also helped refine a KTM RC16 that at one point had the reputation of being perhaps MotoGP's most recalcitrant machine.

But eventually Pedrosa stepped away from wildcards entirely and also stepped into more of a secondary tester role, emphasising work on rideability while new tester Pol Espargaro became the focal point for performance work.

And with KTM's new 850cc bike for the 2027 regulations now being readied for its debut, Pedrosa - who has also earned acclaim as a TV pundit for Spanish broadcaster DAZN - is ceasing his participation in the KTM project.
