title: Hankook's bid for F1 tyre supply - what you need to know
author: Jon Noble
text:
Hankook has begun a Formula 1 tyre testing programme and opened talks with teams as it prepares to bid on becoming grand prix racing’s official supplier from 2029, The Race has learned.

F1’s current contract with Pirelli runs until the end of 2028, after the Italian company won F1’s most recent tender deal, which covered the period from 2025-2027, against a rival bid from Bridgestone.

Its contract was extended by a further season in June this year after an option was taken up by the FIA.

From 2029, however, a new tender process is set to be launched by the FIA and there looks set to be fresh competition to secure the right to be the official F1 supplier.

It is understood that Pirelli wants to wait to see details of the tender before deciding if it enters the fray to extend its current spell which stretches back to 2011, while Bridgestone has long evaluated an F1 return with representatives having attended races.

However, it has now emerged that Hankook is ready to throw its hat into the ring too and has been secretly ramping up its own efforts.

Representatives of the company were spotted at the recent Las Vegas Grand Prix, which was understood to have been their second visit to an F1 race this year following a trip to Madrid in September.

The Race understands that Hankook has used these trips to meet a majority of teams and discuss plans with bosses, CEOs and other senior executives.

The trips to races, which also included visits to events in China, Japan and Singapore in 2025, are only one side of its efforts to get ready for 2029, however.

It is understood that Hankook has already committed a 44-person task force within the company to prepare for an F1 entry.

Beyond committing research and development capability plus simulator running, it has this year completed two development tests for F1 rubber using a modified F2-equivalent-mule car to evaluate potential construction as well as different compounds.

A third test has been scheduled to work on its wet-weather rubber, which it hopes can also help it develop a tyre that features a narrower spray plume to reduce visibility problems caused in wet conditions.

Hankook is also working hard on production and manufacturing planning that would be required to supply F1, F2 and F3 tyres that would come under the umbrella of any tyre tender contract.

Hankook is certainly no stranger to FIA competition, with the South Korean company already the official tyre supplier to the World Rally Championship and has just ended its supply to Formula E where Bridgestone is taking over for the upcoming season. Earlier this year Hankook was also named as a global partner of the governing body.

The period of the new F1 tyre tender beyond 2029 will almost certainly cover the transition to the next rules era, with F1 setting sights on new lighter and nimbler cars to coincide with the switch to V8 power units from 2030.

The plans are also set to include a new tyre design, which is set to reduce wheel size slightly from the current 18-inch design.

title: ‘I told it to never call me again’: AI bots wreak havoc with UK restaurant bookings
author: Helena Horton
text:
Meta claims its Muse assistant will make users’ lives easier, but business owners say AI is driving them to go analogue

R estaurant owners are battling a horde of AI bots and returning to using the telephone instead of online booking as new virtual assistants launch in the UK – but sometimes even that isn’t enough to stop them.

This week, Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta launched its Muse AI assistant in the UK and is encouraging users to let it shop and make restaurant reservations. The bot is given access to the user’s email if they give it permission, and it can make restaurant bookings and go shopping on the user’s behalf.

Muse has been downloaded millions of times in the US, but it has caused chaos for restaurants. The online booking platform Resy has banned bots after restaurants on the platform were swarmed with agents that can refresh the page thousands of times and snap up all the reservations. Now, AI agents are plaguing venues in the UK.

Dave Strauss, the co-owner of Bouchon Racine, which was recently crowned UK restaurant of the year , said he had already had an argument with a would-be diner’s AI bot.

He answers the phones in his French restaurant every day from 11am to take reservation requests and said recently he received an unnerving call: “The other day I answered the phone to an AI bot that sounded very realistic. There was something a bit wrong about it – it sounded exactly like a human being, but something was off. I asked if it was a bot and it said: ‘Yes this is an AI booking process.’”

Strauss added: “I had an argument with the AI bot and told it to never call me again. But that wasn’t very satisfying as it didn’t argue back.”

Kimberley Coke, a high-end restaurant concierge, is paid by celebrities to secure a good table at top dining spots. She said she was worried about the swarm of AI bots: “I think it is terrifying and it could cause absolute chaos.”

Coke, who makes all her bookings via WhatsApp or phone calls, added: “There is now so much information you can get online about the hottest restaurants and where to go, and it is really hard to get the tables and that is why people come to me as I have personal relationships with the restaurants. With the apps, you don’t know who the client is, you have no background on who is coming in, they still might not show up. There is nothing worse for a restaurant in December when they have empty tables.”

Meta has claimed that its product can make people’s lives easier, but that has not been the case for the restaurants on the receiving end of the calls, emails and reservation app bookings.

The problem has been pronounced in New York City, where hard-to-secure restaurant tables are a status symbol. One of the most popular is 4 Charles Prime Rib, which serves a famous double wagyu cheeseburger, often served topped with a fried egg. It has been a popular target for AI agents, with sources at Resy saying they were having to ban multiple accounts using bots to book reservations there.

Strauss said: “There has been a constant shift to make everything as automated as possible to save a bit of money. We believe here that doesn’t work. We get a lot of emails now saying we can outsource our bookings and phone calls to AI. That makes us more keen on doing it the way that we do it. If I could get rid of online booking, I would.”

Jeremy King, who owns Simpson’s in the Strand , Arlington and the Park, said that the move towards depersonalising interactions by using AI was making him go “more analogue” in his restaurants – diners will find it much easier to snag a prime table at one of his venues by picking up the phone.

He said: “I am very happy to embrace new technology but ultimately if it conspires against us we will have to return to managing without.”

Such agents are likely to become more common in the UK and Meta has deals with an array of British businesses – including Marks & Spencer, Currys, Sainsbury’s and easyJet – allowing Muse to navigate their websites more easily and to access their apps. If a company does not offer a “connector” app that Muse can visit, the agent will access its website instead.

The Information Commissioner’s Office and the Competition and Markets Authority said they had been in talks with Meta before Muse’s launch about its responsibility to comply with UK laws. The ICO, the UK’s data protection watchdog, said on Tuesday the tech company had committed to a “voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme”, while the CMA said talks had resulted in changes to make the app’s terms and conditions fairer

Butcher blames costs for closure after 127 years
text:
A family butcher's shop has blamed rising costs as it prepares to close later after 127 years.

Bennett Butchers, in Spalding, Lincolnshire, was opened by Henry Bennett in 1899 and is now owned by Andrew Parsons, his great-grandson.

Parsons said the shop in Winsover Road was still popular and profitable, but a number of issues meant its future was "unviable".

"We're a labour-intensive business. We're also high energy users. The hike in National Insurance from the government last year and all these [things], they all make it very, very difficult," he added.

"We're still a profitable business, but we're not as profitable as we were. And we've reached a point where we need to invest a lot of money in the business to drive it forward."

A spokesperson for HM Treasury said the government was providing "business rates support and action to cut costs for firms".

It was "doubling" the Employment Allowance, which allows employers to reduce their annual National Insurance liability, to £10,500, and ensuring electricity bills were "being cut by up to 25% for over 10,000 eligible businesses".

Parsons thanked the town's residents for the "outpouring of love" shown to the business since it announced the closure on 18 October.

He said the shop had "sold more meat over the last six weeks than we would over two Christmases".

"I just can't thank everybody enough for how they've rallied round and supported us over the last six weeks and filled their freezers," he said.

He also thanked the shop's staff, who he had "been amazing", despite facing redundancy, and said he was relieved many of them now had new jobs.

As well as customers visiting the shop and commenting on social media, an anonymous individual has paid homage to the business with a plaque.

Parsons said it "arrived unannounced on Wednesday evening" and described the wording, which celebrates the shop's long-standing customer service, as "fantastic" and "amazing".

The butcher said he was planning to "relax" after the shop's closure as it was "the first Christmas that I haven't worked for 44 years", but he was not planning to retire just yet and hoped to stay in the meat industry.

title: Village plea for replacement Royal Mail postbox hits the rocks (literally)
author: Anna Tims
text:
Residents woke up to find their vital box missing, but despite 11 months of lobbying the company now says it cannot replace it

Residents of a remote Devon village now have to drive more than a mile to send letters after their attempts to get a new postbox literally hit the rocks.

Villagers in North Huish have described a farcical near 11-month battle to challenge Royal Mail’s excuses after their box vanished without warning last January.

Royal Mail has now informed them the box will not be replaced because the ground is too stony.

The residents fear that their vanishing postbox is part of a move by Royal Mail to reduce collections.

A number of communities have complained that their postal deliveries have been cut after the regulator Ofcom relaxed Royal Mail’s performance targets last year. Ofcom is now investigating claims that parcel deliveries are being prioritised over letters after nearly a quarter of first-class mail failed to arrive on time.

The saga started in January when Royal Mail claimed that the box had been found on the ground and was beyond repair as its supporting post had rotted.

After initially agreeing to replace it after villagers’ complaints, it incorrectly claimed that the site was privately owned and it could not proceed.

It subsequently blamed a council administration fee, and then a nearby parking area, for preventing reinstatement, before announcing that loose stones on the site made installation impossible.

North Huish parish council offered to buy the postbox-sized plot of land to speed up the process, and a local farmer has volunteered to install a new supporting post, but Royal Mail has refused to budge. “We initially thought the box had been stolen when it suddenly went missing,” says North Huish resident Lesley Ring.

“It was used regularly and none of us had ever noticed that it was unstable. In the light of subsequent events, we think Royal Mail just came and took it.”

Royal Mail initially told villagers that the replacement process would take up to four months.

“It cited the need for breaking ground permits, permission from landowners, compliance checks, underground utility checks and health and safety checks,” Ring says.

“We were extremely surprised at the apparent red tape involved and, over the following months, Royal Mail seemed to gradually go back on its word and came up with a variety of obstacles.”

In August, residents were told all options had been exhausted because the site of the original box, alongside a public telephone kiosk, was privately owned and no alternatives could be found.

Royal Mail declined to check ownership of the plot because it would have to pay Devon county council a £72 search fee for the service, and it declared the case closed.

The council agreed to perform the search for free to break the impasse, and confirmed that the plot was on a public highway.

Royal Mail then declared that loose stones and uneven ground had forced it to cancel the project.

Villagers were told that they could hand any letters for posting to their postal worker during a delivery round, provided there was capacity to carry it.

“We rarely see a postman as we tend to get post in one or two bundles a week,” says Ring. “The nearest box is over half an hour’s walk away, which puts it out of reach of elderly and disabled people who can’t drive.”

Ring says service failures are affecting her long-distance relationship. “My partner and I have conducted our relationship largely by post for 27 years, and we write to each other constantly, with a phone call on a Sunday,” she says.

“Too often recently, the conversation is hampered by the fact that letters have been held up from week to week, despite the fact that we only use so-called first-class post.”

Royal Mail says: “We understand how important it is for residents in North Huish to be able to post letters close to home, and we’re sorry we haven’t been able to replace the village postbox.

“The old box fell when the wooden post supporting it rotted. We planned to put a replacement in the same spot, but our engineer found that the uneven ground and damaged kerb raised safety concerns.

“We looked at other locations nearby but couldn’t find a safe, accessible spot on public land.”

Royal Mail told us that “there are alternatives at Beneckowle, about three-quarters of a mile from the old site, and at Diptford, about a mile away”.

When the Guardian checked these distances using route planners, this indicated both of these locations were about a 1.3-mile drive away.

“We recognise that neither is as convenient as having a postbox in the village, so we’re also arranging for residents to be able to hand stamped letters to their postie when they receive a delivery,” it adds.

title: Grand Theft Anthropic: how GTA can inspire a fightback against AI | Alexander Hurst
author: Alexander Hurst
text:
Tech billionaires are taking us for a ride. But new ‘poison pill’ software could help shield human-made creative output from hijacking

Grand Theft Auto VI came out on the same day that Anthropic made its stock market debut. I keep thinking about that coincidence. As more than one tech writer has pointed out, the new GTA took 13 years to make, more than $1bn of investment and involved 9,000 sets of human hands, and it will probably be the last blockbuster video game to be fully free of generative AI.

On the day of its release, a group chat with my most gaming-minded male friends erupted in discussion about whether or not video games, and GTA VI specifically, rose to the level of art. Exploring a national park? Yes, that’s there . Badly assemble a coffee table from “Krapea” (the game’s fictional furniture company)? Ditto. Eating a hot dog? Why not. All of it gloriously human in origin. Perhaps that in itself is an argument for how GTA VI crosses the blurry line from entertainment to something more. It is a medium by which human beings offer others a (necessarily incomplete) interpretation of what it’s like to be them in the world, or to try to transcend it.

title: ‘The key is pricing realistically’: how to sell your home in a falling market
author: Sandra Haurant
text:
From small fixes such as decluttering to taking your property off the market for a break, there are ways to seal the deal

Selling your home is always a big task, but when the headlines are telling you prices are falling, it can feel even more daunting.

Average house prices in the UK fell by 1.2% over the year to 31 October, according to Lloyds bank – the steepest drop since late 2023.

Plus there are fewer people buying: in September, mortgage approvals for house purchase were down by 19.4% year on year, the most recent official data shows.

So just how worried should sellers be? “It is most certainly getting more difficult to sell a property in the UK,” says Stuart Ducker, the strategic solutions director at the property data company TwentyCi.

Of the homes on market between January and October this year, 53.5% have been sold so far, Ducker says.

“But there are areas of the country – for example, inner London – where the chances of a sale are only 30%.

“In terms of property types, the flats market is not great at the minute: the likelihood of selling a flat nationally is only 41% in 2026 to date.”

House prices in Greater London are down by 3.1% year on year, according to the latest Lloyds data, while south-east and south-west England have recorded falls of 2.4% over the year.

But in some other parts of the UK, prices have been going up, albeit more slowly than before. Northern Ireland, for example, experienced average property values rising by 4.4% in the year to the end of October.

And within regions it is a mixed picture. “Even in some of those more challenging parts of the market, there are still areas where there’s a shortage of stock,” says Emily Williams, the director of research at Savills estate agents.

She adds: “In outer London there’s still decent demand that has not been met by good available stock for family housing. So, if you’ve got a good family house, there are still buyers out there looking.”

Things could be more problematic if you are selling your home in the south of England and buying a new home in a region where prices are still rising, as your buying power may be reduced.

Others who stand to lose out when prices fall are sellers who do not plan to buy another property, or downsizers who are relying on a set amount of equity to fund their retirement, or help family members.

However, for those moving within the same region, a fall might work in their favour.

“What matters is the gap between the home being sold and the home being bought, not the headline price of either,” says Nick Mendes, the technical manager at the mortgage broker John Charcol. “Those trading up are often in the strongest position when prices are softening.”

Whatever your situation and wherever you are in the country, finding a buyer quickly depends on getting the price right.

It is most important to price “realistically” at the outset, Williams says. “Buyers are very savvy. Everyone can look at Rightmove or Zoopla and see what things have sold for previously.”

The trouble is, it can be very difficult to know what the right price is. Typically, a seller might ask three or four estate agents to come and value their home – but they may all come up with different valuations that vary by many thousands of pounds.

As well as checking recently sold properties in your area, on portals such as Rightmove and Zoopla, it is also worth challenging the agents to justify their valuations.

Alex Oppenheim, a director at John D Wood estate agents, says: “Ask the agents to show their recent comparable evidence. Can they show you similar properties that they have actually sold in that price range in the past few months?”

Agents might say they have buyers looking for a property similar to yours, and it is perfectly possible to test the waters.

Oppenheim says: “You can agree for them to market your property to those buyers, without putting it on the portals to begin with, to see if there is any interest. You can even say, ‘If you get a buyer at that figure, I will give you an extra 0.5%’.”

Then, if that doesn’t work, you can think about listing the property for sale with a lower price.

It can be demoralising to have a stream of viewers coming through the door and no offers. It could be easy to think there is something wrong with the property. Perhaps if you repainted, or changed the carpets, or did something with the kitchen, it might help? Oppenheim suggests that is rarely the solution.

But there may be some simple things you can do to make a difference.

Creating a sense of light and space by clearing away clutter and cleaning the windows is always a good idea, as is generally maintaining the property even when you are trying to sell it.

“I would recommend spending on things that fall under the category of maintenance. So if, for example, you have repaired a leak and there is still some evidence of the old damage on the ceiling, you should absolutely get that repainted,” Oppenheim says.

“But you could spend thousands on cosmetic changes, and it will probably make no difference. There is a misconception about problems with properties languishing on the market for a long time without finding a buyer. There is typically nothing wrong with those properties – the only thing that is wrong is the price.”

Sam Molyneux-Summers, the chief operating officer at the estate agents Century 21, says buyers dictate the market.

“We always ask for feedback after viewings, including what people think about the price,” he says. “If we are consistently hearing that people think it is too high, we will suggest lowering it.”

The problem is that lowering it can, in itself, make it harder to sell. Research from Savills, which focused on houses with asking prices above £1m, shows that where a property did not need a price cut, it took about eight weeks to sell. Where there was at least one cut, it took about 13 weeks longer. And if you needed two or more, it took an additional 16 weeks.…

title: Stunted sprouts: heatwaves and drought take toll on festive vegetable
author: Joanna Partridge
text:
The Christmas staple is smaller this year after a hot, dry summer hit the water-loving – but versatile – brassica

They are a key ingredient in many Christmas dinners, but brussels sprouts appearing on diners’ plates this festive season are likely to be smaller than usual, after the hot, dry summer took its toll on the water-loving crop.

Sprouts are generally planted outdoors between March and early June, meaning they were already in the ground when the UK faced a series of heatwaves and drought conditions across Wales and most of England.

Low water-reserves limited the amount growers could use to irrigate their crops, slowing down the growth of sprouts and other brassica such as cabbages, broccoli and cauliflowers.

Sprouts grow on a stalk, maturing from the bottom upwards. This means the largest sprouts are found at the bottom, with the smallest at the top. Supermarkets and other food retailers generally select only the mid-sized sprouts, found in the middle.

Higher volumes of stunted sprouts are available this year after a challenging growing season, according to the low-waste food retailer Oddbox, which is known for supplying wonky fruit and vegetables.

“We would typically see smaller sprouts heading to Oddbox, because that’s the product that growers don’t tend to have outlets for, but this year there’s an awful lot more of them,” said Gavin Phelps, the company’s head of sourcing.

Most of the sprouts available are from Lincolnshire, where quantities of brassica and other crops are grown, but which has had extended periods of drought.

Some consumers may believe that smaller sprouts will be harder to peel than larger ones, making the much-maligned vegetable more difficult to prepare.

Phelps said this was not the case: “Peeling small sprouts is of course going to be a bit of extra effort, but you can also save some prep time because you don’t need to cut them in half like you typically do with the larger size ones. So it equals out.”

Sprouts are harvested in the UK between September and March, although a quarter of their annual consumption takes place in the two weeks leading up to Christmas.

Growers say that tweaks to sprout breeding and the introduction of new varieties have made the vegetable – sometimes criticised for perceived bitterness – tastier. More than half of adults (56.4%) polled by YouGov in October said they liked sprouts , while the number who said they disliked them has fallen from 26% to under 22% in the past six years.

Cooking techniques have also improved, said Phelps. “Back 20 or 30 years ago there was this obsession with boiling everything. I feel people have come round to them more because there is just so much more out there in terms of recipe inspiration.”

Cooks may want to try roasting, pickling or even smashing sprouts this Christmas, while Phelps is planning to crisp his in an air fryer.

title: Palestinian tells of ‘devastating’ struggle after being made redundant by EU in Gaza
author: Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent
text:
Mohammad Baraka unable to access redundancy pay for almost 20 years’ service as family’s situation becomes ‘increasingly desperate’

A Palestinian man who worked for the EU in Gaza has told of a “devastating” struggle to survive after he was made redundant by bosses in Brussels.

He was let go last year after being evacuated to Egypt but his redundancy payment was made to an account to which he has no access. “My family’s situation has become increasingly desperate,” said Mohammad Baraka, a former staffer at the EU border assistance mission (EUBam).

“Both of my daughters have suffered severe psychological distress as a result of the war, displacement and the prolonged uncertainty surrounding our future.”

The 220,000 Israeli shekels (£52,000) payment for almost 20 years’ service was made on 5 August last year to the Bank of Palestine but access to the money has been blocked, a risk he was aware of given the relatively large sum being transferred.

He said he wrote on several occasions to the European Commission , asking it not to make the payment into that bank because of a known risk that a large sum of money could be misconstrued as war funds. “I am now in the devastating position of having money in my name that I cannot access, while my family is experiencing severe financial hardship,” said Baraka.

Instead he had asked for the payment to go to a new account in an Abu Dhabi bank, but that never materialised.

Baraka was evacuated in 2023 after his house in Gaza was bombed and family members killed. The EU tried to relocate him to alternative offices in the West Bank but travel for Palestinians in Gaza was severely restricted. After a hasty three-day concession agreed with the Egyptian government, Baraka was able to leave for Cairo.

As the conflict continued, Baraka was initially able to work remotely from Cairo as an EU employee and had the comfort of a salary, private healthcare and access to schools for his two children. But when Brussels decided to close its EUBam office in Rafah, he was let go, leading to what he says have been traumatic consequences for himself and his wife and two daughters.

He says the evacuation to Egypt with no plan for onward travel to an EU nation or a diplomatically secured place in another country has rendered him stateless, with no residency rights and no right to healthcare or schooling for his seriously ill wife and two daughters, both of whom he says are suffering from the trauma of war.

One of his daughters has an acute mental health condition and Baraka says he cannot pay for her treatment. “I am not asking for charity or special treatment. I am asking for access to my own money, and for accountability over a decision that could have been avoided,” said Baraka.

“I had specifically asked the [EU] mission to transfer my money to my new bank account in Egypt to avoid precisely this situation,” he said.

“If the EU argues that it fulfilled its obligations simply because it transferred the settlement, I believe the legitimate question is whether an employer can consider its responsibility discharged when it knowingly disregards an employee’s repeated warnings about the destination of such a substantial payment.”

Last year he wrote to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen , pleading with her to reverse what he called his “unjust dismissal” and asked her to restore his employment, even temporarily, “until a dignified and legal solution is arranged”.

He also wrote to the European ombudsman to ask them to open an investigation but they replied last week to say they had no scope for an inquiry. “We fully appreciate that you and your family are in an immensely difficult position. The hardship you are experiencing as a result of the war and your displacement are clear from your complaint,” wrote Tina Nilsson, the head of inquiries.

“I realise that this conclusion will be disappointing. I nevertheless hope you can understand why, based on the information available, there are insufficient grounds for the ombudsman to intervene further.”

He is now suing the commission for alleged breach of Belgian employment law but the case could take years to be heard.

Without the “laissez-passer” document that allowed him to be evacuated from Gaza, he cannot leave Egypt, he says, putting him in an impossible position.

A spokesperson for the commission said: “Due to the ongoing related court case, we cannot comment on this further.”

title: La succession: France’s wealthiest family said to be battling over who will take over LVMH
author: Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
text:
Bernard Arnault’s children – described as ‘modern-day French royals’ – are subject of rivalry rumours over who will succeed him

They are France’s richest family, leading the world’s biggest luxury goods empire, dressed in matching Dior suits – a clan so powerful they have been described as modern-day French royals.

But in recent months, the family dynasty of Bernard Arnault , 77, the billionaire head of the LVMH group whose brands range from Louis Vuitton handbags to Tiffany jewellery, has become the subject of speculation about internal rivalry over which of his children could take over the company.

This week it emerged that the health-conscious Arnault, who likes to play tennis with the Swiss champion Roger Federer, can continue to lead the family holding company until he is 95, according to a new filing, pushing back any decisions on his succession.

Last year, the age cap of Arnault’s chief executive role at LVMH was raised to 85 to allow him to stay on in the position. The fashion tycoon once joked about still leading the business at 100.

The question of which of Arnault’s five adult children could eventually lead the family company is seen as key to the French economy and the political class.

LVMH, which has more than 75 brands including fashion, perfumes and champagne, is a big employer in France.

Arnault, nicknamed the “wolf in cashmere” for his acquisitions of leading brands and whose personal wealth is estimated at more than $100bn, owns almost all of France’s business and economic press as well as the daily newspaper Le Parisien and the celebrity magazine Paris Match.

He attended Donald Trump’s second inauguration, as a personal friend, and is regularly present at official French state dinners with world leaders.

This month, Émilie Lanez published an account of what she called the emotional tensions inside the Arnault family’s unresolved succession challenge, based on what she said were hours of off-record conversations with insiders. “I was really struck by the family’s ethereal, otherworldly nature: they are like deities in a performance, and France is a spectator,” she said.

The book, Monsieur et les siens, now in discussion over a possible publication in English, traces the family’s story from Arnault’s childhood in Roubaix, in the former industrial heartland of northern France, where he took over his family’s building company before moving into property development and then luxury goods.

Lanez describes Arnault’s wife, the classical pianist Hélène Mercier-Arnault, working out on her treadmill in the early morning watching the HBO series Succession about a family business power-struggle, and then being at pains to publicly deny any rift or friction among the Arnault children.

The book depicts Arnault’s deep personal involvement in his children’s education. Schooling was so important in his own upbringing that when at age 10 he said farewell to his grandfather at his funeral, he put his glowing school report card into his grandfather’s clasped hands in his coffin.

When he had two children with his first wife, Anne Dewavrin, he devised a system to personally teach his daughter Delphine to read at a young age. At 51, she is now the chief executive of Christian Dior Couture, one of the most important roles at LVMH. Her brother Antoine, 49, has an important communications role, running the group’s image and environmental strategy.

Arnault later married Mercier-Arnault and had three more sons who all work for LVMH brands. Alexandre, 34, is deputy chief executive of the drinks brand Moët Hennessy; Frédéric, 32, runs the luxury fashion brand Loro Piana ; and Jean, 28, is watch director at Louis Vuitton.

When the youngest three were teenagers and preparing for higher education, Lanez writes that Arnault personally hired and interviewed tutors. The boys would come home from their day’s classes, then study with a tutor from 8pm to 11pm then go to their father’s room so he could ask them about the equations they had been tackling.

“They are likened to royals because of the power and influence they have in France,” said Lanez. “And also because they have a kind of court, courtesans and counsellors. It’s a dynasty, and the children, particularly the three youngest, have been raised to perpetuate the empire.”

Just as Arnault as a child would be shown round his father’s family building business, he regularly took his own children, and then grandchildren, on his favourite weekend activity: inspecting his luxury shops.

Arnault is aware that any family divisions can make a company vulnerable. This year, when Mercier-Arnault was promoting her latest classical music record, she did a high-profile round of media interviews in France, seeking to reassure that there were no rifts between the five children.

But with the Arnaults’ vast wealth often cited as an example of the growing power of billionaires in France amid widening economic inequality, Mercier-Arnault’s comments were scrutinised.

French media reported that in an edited radio segment she had said that being homeless could be seen as a “lifestyle choice”.

Mercier-Arnault said later on a TV show that there had been a misunderstanding and she had been referring to her experience as the carer of her late sister, a violinist who was bipolar and had died by suicide, and who had begun a relationship with a person who was homeless. She told the newspaper Libération she was “deeply sorry”.

The cast of characters in the Arnault clan includes another high-profile and influential French billionaire, the telecoms executive Xavier Niel , who is the life-partner of Delphine Arnault. The couple have two children.

“The arrival of Xavier Niel in this family was like a theatrical scenario,” Lanez said, comparing the family saga to a novel.

Asked by the Guardian to comment on the book and speculation of tension or rivalry over the succession, LVMH declined to comment.…

title: AI labs sitting on ‘bombshell’ revelations that could cause global chaos, experts warn
author: Aisha Down
text:
Exclusive: AI may have cracked decades-old maths problems that underpin encryption at banks and government agencies

AI companies are sitting on “bombshell” revelations that could disrupt a cornerstone of security for banks and governments in as soon as a few months, leading experts believe.

Scott Aaronson, a pre-eminent theoretical computer scientist, told the Guardian there were “well-attested rumours” that powerful artificial intelligence models had broken ground on decades-old maths problems related to how the world encodes secret information.

Depending on what has been discovered, it is possible that hackers – and many other people – could in short order have the power to more easily decrypt the world’s secret communications: banking transactions, diplomatic cables and private emails, for example.

If this happened, then spy agencies, governments, banks and private companies could be forced to very suddenly update the foundations of how they communicate, or risk extremely sensitive information being widely exposed.

Aaronson’s and others’ concerns come from a series of mathematical advances that frontier AI companies have announced in the past weeks.

Most of these are abstract breakthroughs. But to experts in the field, they indicate that AI is powerful enough to crack problems that most of them thought would be unsolved for the foreseeable future.

Earlier this week, Aaronson wrote that he was “virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells [in cryptography]”.

“The people who thought AI couldn’t do any interesting maths are definitely wrong at this stage, and so it’s no longer clear where the limit is,” said Steven Murdoch, a professor of computer science at University College London.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday, the mathematician Marcus du Sautoy said “we don’t know” what the broader ramifications of many of these discoveries were, and what this meant for encryption.

But, he added, “no one has been talking about the problem which is at the heart of protecting all our electronic secrets. Why is nobody talking about that problem? Some of us are thinking: maybe they’ve already solved it, and of course, it would have such massive implications that everyone has just kept it quiet.”

Governments, banks and spy agencies have been preparing for the possibility of powerful decryption for the past few years. This is because quantum computers, when developed, will be able to break the decades-old algorithms that underpin many forms of encryption.

But the timeline for quantum computers to be able to do this is still years away, not weeks or months. Murdoch said many governments and technology companies were working towards a higher standard of encryption – one that would not be vulnerable to quantum computers – but slowly. “The target was something like 2032, and that was probably going to be missed.”

Now he, Aaronson and others think there may be sudden advances in what the world understands about cryptography, and these could come soon.

What these revelations could be is less certain. What Aaronson and others think could have happened is that either AI has come up with a new way to break encryption or, conversely, it has proved that such a shortcut does not exist.

This would come from AI models picking apart the maths that underlies encryption, and that up until this point has not been fully understood. If AI has done this, it could find a way to decrypt, and therefore expose, massive amounts of secret data.

It could also prove this information is more secure than previously thought.

The world uses multiple forms of encryption – based on different underlying algorithms – and there are different guesses as to what may have been found, and therefore what systems could be affected.

No concrete announcements have come from AI companies regarding revelations about encryption, said Aaronson, but “anyone informed is assuming” that they are there.

Alan Woodward, a professor of computer science at the University of Surrey, said a mathematical breakthrough related to cryptography would not necessarily mean widespread chaos tomorrow. What has changed is the speed at which AI is solving problems that have been shrouded in mystery for decades – with potentially serious consequences.

“What [Aaronson] is basically saying is that people need to be ready for something to suddenly spring out, because there’s definitely a sort of a trend.”

Earlier this week, Andrew Bailey, the governor of the Bank of England, addressed fears that companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic had achieved breakthroughs in cryptography, saying these companies should be cautious about releasing new models to the public.

In the past weeks, AI companies have released proofs of mathematical results that closely relate to this question. One of these involved a foundational question about how to categorise computationally “hard” problems.

Aaronson said these breakthroughs had been seismic for experts in the fields of maths and computer science, some of whom have spent their careers working on these problems, and others who assumed that these problems would not be solved in their lifetimes.

“We’ve never seen a period like this,” he said. “I’m trying to face the reality of what is happening.”

He emphasised that these breakthroughs still needed to be understood, however – which means human mathematicians and computer scientists need to go through and verify the proofs that AI companies say they have produced.

Woodward said it was unlikely that any discoveries would “undo encryption by the end of the week”. Even if such a finding exists, there are hurdles to its widespread deployment.

But big banks and governments that rely on encryption “need to be agile”, said Woodward. “The ones that are agile and can change quickly will be safe. The ones that are the laggards could get caught out.”

Anthropic and OpenAI were approached for comment.

title: Could AI break encryption? What mathematical breakthroughs mean for cybersecurity
author: Aisha Down
text:
Experts suggest AI companies may be sitting on ‘bombshell’ that could have severe consequences for secret information

Leading experts and the governor of the Bank of England have suggested that top AI companies might have something under their hat – a “bombshell” revelation about encryption. Depending on what it is, it could have major consequences for the world’s secret information, and the banks and governments that hold and transmit it.

This is because of recent, startling mathematical advances made by AI models, which are still being understood.

Some of the problems that have been solved relate to cryptography. Some are significant and have been the subject of entire careers.

Leading computer scientists think that, if AI has broken ground on these problems, it is overwhelmingly likely it has, or will soon, produce revelations about the core mathematics behind encoding the world’s information.

Scott Aaronson, a preeminent computer scientist, cited a recent proof – from Anthropic and OpenAI – that VP≠VNP, a finding that he says has led him to drink uncharacteristic amounts of wine in his kitchen.

In basic terms, this proof is about what problems can be solved easily by the computers we have, and what problems are truly “hard” problems – meaning that the world’s most powerful computers could not solve them in, say, a lifetime.

Theoretical computer scientists are interested in this question: are all problems in the world quickly solvable with good enough algorithms, or are there problems that might take vast amounts of time to solve, and for which no shortcuts are possible?

Anthropic and OpenAI’s proof that VP≠VNP is a major step forward in answering this question, which was first posed in the 1970s. While it concerns a slightly different problem from breaking encryption, it suggests that AI models can work ably in this territory and produce groundbreaking results.

The world was abuzz over the summer with claims new, powerful AI models – such as Mythos – were capable of finding hundreds of vulnerabilities in lines of code.

Put one way, this amounts to finding lots of grammatical errors in the language of computers. It isn’t particularly difficult, but artificial intelligence can do it well. AI can also help cyber-attackers find these errors and exploit them.

Breaking encryption is a far more fundamental challenge. It means making a novel mathematical discovery, which stands to illuminate our conceptual understanding of how computers work.

Encryption is based on the idea that some maths problems are too “hard” for computers to break, no matter how many GPUs you shove into a datacentre. But this is a very abstract thing to argue.

Governments, banks and tech companies have been updating the encryption they use in anticipation of powerful quantum computers coming online. Their new methods – or old methods – may be resilient to decryption algorithms.

If they were not resilient, and a decryption algorithm were discovered, that algorithm could still be difficult to implement in practice.

Still, the extreme scenario is vast amounts of information, from Swift bank transfers to the private messages of government officials could suddenly be read by those who could access it. This could include secure exchanges from decades ago.

Many intelligence agencies put listening devices on cables to collect information transmitted through them. One example is GCHQ. Such agencies may not have been able to crack this information up to now, but that could suddenly change.

title: Yuri and I used to play football together. Then I spotted his name among Russia’s war dead
author: Pjotr Sauer
text:
I had no idea he had gone to fight in Ukraine and without hacked data I would probably never have learned of his death

One evening, after weeks spent counting Russia’s war dead, I began looking for names I might recognise.

My colleagues and I had been working our way through more than 11m death certificates leaked from Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, and identifying nearly half a million Russian soldiers who had died in the war in Ukraine.

We had sorted the dead by age, region and cause of death, building the most detailed picture yet of Russia’s losses in nearly five years of war.

Now I typed in the names of the places where I had grown up.

My childhood was spent in Rublevka, a stretch of pine forest west of Moscow that has been home to the Russian elite since Soviet times. With the collapse of communism and Russia’s chaotic embrace of capitalism, the dachas of party officials gave way to the sprawling estates of oligarchs.

Vladimir Putin and Dmitry Medvedev established their residences in Rublevka. In more recent years, the area has become a refuge for ousted leaders, among them Ukraine’s Viktor Yanukovych and, as the Guardian previously reported , Syria’s Bashar al-Assad.

I did not expect to find many names there.

Our analysis had shown just how unevenly the burden of the war had fallen across Russian society. In some of the poorest regions, working-age men were up to 32 times more likely to die in the war than men of the same age in Moscow. I knew sons of the Russian elite who had left the country shortly after the invasion, keen to avoid being called up to fight.

My village, Zhukovka, returned no results.

I worked my way along the Rublyovo-Uspenskoye highway, the well-paved road connecting the wealthy settlements west of Moscow. Here and there, a lone death certificate appeared.

Then I typed in Gorki-10, a town a few miles further down the road, named after the famed writer Maxim Gorky, who spent his final years there.

One of the names on my screen was instantly familiar: Yuri Vladimirovich Kyrmyz, aged 31.

Place of death: Makiivka, Svatove district, in the Russian-occupied Luhansk region of Ukraine . Cause of death on 3 February 2025: an explosion during military operations.

Makiivka, a small village on the banks of the Zherebets River, had been the scene of months of bitter fighting as Russian forces sought to retake territory lost during Ukraine’s 2022 counteroffensive.

Two decades earlier, Yuri and I used to play football together as teenagers.

Though we were never particularly close, he was a reliable presence at our games, a quiet, unassuming defender who rarely had much to say. We had not spoken in years. Until that evening, I had no idea he had gone to fight in Ukraine, let alone that he had died there.

I also do not know what made him join Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Kremlin has worked hard to insulate Moscow and its suburbs from the war. In neighbouring Barvikha, at the Luxury Village shopping complex, visitors can still buy a Ferrari or a Chanel handbag, despite western sanctions. But for all its associations with wealth and power, Rublevka is also home to another Russia.

Parts of Gorki-10 consist of Soviet-era blocks of flats, built for families who serviced the rich or toiled at the local stud farm, which dates back to the 19th century. I remembered that Yuri’s family was not well-off. Before enlisting, Yuri worked as a car dealer.

The signing bonuses and salaries offered by the Russian military, in some cases amounting to several times the average annual wage, would have represented a life-changing sum of money.

Yuri was one of millions of Russians of our generation who grew up immersed in the memory of the Soviet victory over Nazi Germany. Victory Day, on 9 May, was one of the biggest occasions of the year, rivalled only by New Year’s Eve. Over the past two decades, Putin has appropriated that collective memory, telling a new generation of Russians that in Ukraine they are fighting the same “Nazi” enemy their grandfathers once faced.

Until I discovered Yuri’s name in the database, the only person I knew to have joined the invasion, other than the soldiers I had interviewed in the course of my reporting, was my former football coach Andrei Solomatin.

In his prime, Solomatin had played for CSKA and Lokomotiv Moscow, won 13 caps for Russia and appeared in all three of the country’s matches at the 2002 World Cup.

But his life unravelled after retirement. There were debts, problems with alcohol and a gradual slide into obscurity. By the time I met him, the former international footballer was eking out a modest living coaching our local Sunday league team.

Our team was an eclectic collection of nationalities, including Dutch (me), British and Nigerian players. I cannot recall Solomatin ever expressing hostility towards Ukraine. Politics, as far as I could tell, did not concern him.

In autumn 2022, he began delivering aid to Española, a far-right military formation drawn from the ranks of Russian football ultras fighting in occupied Ukraine. By July 2023, he had joined the unit himself.

He was back on television, this time in military fatigues. In interviews, he spoke of his “complete trust” in Putin. The war appears to have given him a sense of public importance he had not enjoyed for years.

Yuri, like hundreds of thousands of other Russian soldiers who have died in Ukraine, left little public trace. Had hackers not obtained the records of Russia’s state statistics agency, I would probably never have learned of his death.

Although in some of the worst-affected parts of Russia nearly everyone knows someone who has died in the war, the full scale of the losses remains hidden from the Russian public.

Asked about the military deaths on Wednesday, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, dismissed the findings, insisting that only official data could be trusted.…

title: Yankees news: Black Friday Shopping
author: John Griffin
text:
The Yankees eyeing Padres’ catchers; Chisholm bolts for AL East rival, Yarbrough for Cubs; ranking pitcher contracts

MLB Trade Rumors | Mark Polishuk : Ever since the trade deadline, the Yankees have made it very clear that they have wanted to add to their catching contingent, looking for a right-handed bat to go alongside the lefty-swinging Austin Wells. With San Diego looking to clear a path to playing time for top prospect Ethan Salas, two names that the Yankees have been looking into are Luis Campusano and Freddy Fermin. While both are right-handed hitters, their profiles are remarkably different: Fermin would give the Yankees one of the best defensive tandems in the game, and Campusano would provide some power behind the dish the team has desperately needed in recent years. For what it’s worth, not only have the two teams made some high-profile moves in recent years, the situation very much mimics the 2023-2024 winter: the Padres need rotation help, the Yankees have an excess of starters, and the Padres have exactly what the Yankees need.

ESPN | Jorge Castillo : As Andrew detailed for us yesterday , former Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. agreed to a one-year contract with the Toronto Blue Jays that contains both a player and a team option for 2028 and which guarantees him $34.5 million. The move brings to a close a dramatic Yankees career for the 28-year-old infielder, which saw him provide a spark to a scuffling 2024 squad and become a key contributor at the hot corner as the team went to the World Series for the first time since 2009, fill a critical role in the middle of the order in 2025, before scuffling in his contract year while courting controversy on and off the field.

MLB Trade Rumors | Darragh McDonald : As Friday came to a close, we learned that another multi-year Yankee who hit free agency would not be returning in 2027. Steady long man Ryan Yarbrough is signing with the Cubs, per Robert Murray of FanSided (who also broke the Chisholm news). The Yankees’ decision to sign Brent Suter essentially rendered Yarbrough’s possible future with the team redundant, as Suter has a similar profile and better stuff. Between Suter, Brent Headrick, and Tim Hill, the bullpen was getting fairly left-handed regardless.

The Athletic | Jayson Stark : (subscription required) Following Tarik Skubal’s record-breaking nine-year, $450 million megacontract with the New York Mets, Jayson Stark of The Athletic decided to rank the best and worst free agent contracts ( not extensions) signed by pitchers over the years. Perhaps unsurprisingly, two of the five best belong to the Yankees: CC Sabathia, who led the Yankees to the 2009 World Series in the first year of his deal, and Gerrit Cole, who has won one Cy Young and finished as the runner-up one other time over the first seven years of his deal.

title: Heat 108, Knicks 105: “Really tough to win a poorly coached, corruptly reffed, half rotation injured game.”
author: Russell Richardson
text:
The Knicks (12-7) lost two Emirates NBA Cup games this season but defeated the Cavaliers on Wednesday. Their chances of reaching the next round and continuing their defense of the Cup weren’t nonexistent, but they needed to beat the Heat (11-7) by more than six points and for the Pacers to drop the Sixers.

First things first: the surging Heat are a handful even when New York’s roster is complete. The Knicks had to meet the challenge without OG Anunoby (calf), Andre Drummond (concussion), Miles McBride (groin), and Jordan Clarkson (foot). The remaining players weren’t altogether healthy, either: Karl-Anthony Towns (19 PTS, 10 RBS, 34 MIN) has an abdominal contusion, and Josh Hart (6 PTS, 9 RBS, 8 AST) is playing through a sore knee and shoulder. Our depleted Knickerbockers fell behind in the first quarter, then went down by 23 in the second. They cut their deficit to five in the third frame and had the Heat on the ropes in crunch time. A few missed free throws, an uncalled flagrant foul, and odd coaching decisions let the rally—and their Cup dreams—slip through their fingers. Final score: 108-105.

Quoth DWLLTheKnicksfan: “Really tough to win a poorly coached, corruptly reffed, half rotation injured game. Respect that it was close.”

After the Knicks fell behind 15-7, coach Mike Brown replaced Hart with Pacôme Dadiet (4 PTS, 1 STL, 21 MIN, +7). Pac-Man played arm-flapping defense that disrupted the flow and led to a Miami turnover, then dunked a Brunson pass on the run. We’re starting to see the vision! The French fella stayed on the floor when the next round of swaps came, playing alongside Brunson, Hart, Jose Alvarado (7 PTS, 15 MIN), and James Wiseman (11 PTS). The latter lasted just two minutes and committed a foul that heralded the return of Towns. Not a great first look on a night when Drummond was out.

New York logged nine boards in the first quarter. Giannis Antetokounmpo (22 PTS, 23 RBS, 32 MIN) matched that total alone, scarfing up most of Miami’s 14 boards. A physical game had Towns wincing in pain, and we were wincing at New York’s crappy shooting (2-of-11 from deep). With the Floridians sinking half of their three-pointers, the Knicks trailed 31-21 at the break.

In the second quarter, Mohamed Diawara and the Tylers (Kolek, Nickel) took the floor. Miami scored 12 unanswered while the ’Bockers continued to shoot like the Blind Boys of Alabama. The rookie Nickel looked lost and the coach bewildered. Mike Brown called for time when the score reached 48-27.

Out of that timeout, Brown sent Wiseman and Dadiet back in. Wiseman’s minutes were rough. On consecutive plays, Wiggins picked off his inbound pass for a layup, and then Ryan Conwell intercepted his inbound pass. Unsurprisingly, he suffered a quick hook. Mike was running out of levers to pull as his team fell behind by 23. With four rotation players out and his starters all posting a plus-minus of -13 or worse, the coach fielded 11 different players in the first half in an attempt to slow Erik Spoelstra’s squad, which scored inside, outside, and wherever else it wanted.

Thanks to a spirited late-half nine-oh run, the home team entered halftime trailing 60-44. There was plenty of blame to go around for our heroes. Towns (still painin’!) and Brunson combined for 25 of their team’s 44 points, but the other starters had five points each, and the Knicks’ bench had been outscored by its Miami counterpart, 30-4.

Through the half, the Flamingos shot 45% from the field and 36% from deep (9-of-25), while New York managed 40% and a miserable 21% (4-of-19). The Heat held only slight advantages in rebounds (24-23) and points in the paint (22-18) but were considerably better at protecting the ball. Nine Knicks turnovers yielded 11 Miami points, while the Heat committed just four turnovers that yielded three New York points. Worse, Miami won the battle for second-chance points, 10-0.

Over the first two minutes of the second half, Towns, Bridges, and Shamet combined for nine points to cut the deficit to 61-53. Miami fought back, but New York looked rejuvenated and alert (a marked improvement from the tryptophan blues of the first half). By the midway point of the quarter, the Knicks had converted five straight shots, reducing their deficit to five. As we’ve seen in game after game this season, it takes a lot of energy to climb out of deep holes. As the Knicks faltered, back-to-back Bridges turnovers allowed Giannis and Bam Adebayo (25 PTS, 7 RBS) to hammer Miami’s lead back to 11.

Our heroes got an unexpected lift from Wiseman. He leaped into the fray, scoring seven points on three buckets and a free throw late in the third. That was more like it! Add a Brunson floater and an Antetokounmpo shot-clock violation, and New York trailed 86-79 at the horn.

Bam was a bother to start the fourth, netting two buckets, blocking shots by Shamet and Kolek, and drawing two fouls from Towns. Towns headed to the bench with four fouls at the 8:27 mark. Meanwhile, Shamet, Bridges, and Kolek each contributed layups to keep the Knicks within striking distance. The Heat struggled from the perimeter, with OAKAAKUYOAKs Tim Hardaway Jr. and Bobby Portis blowing opportunities to extend the lead.

Down 91-85 with plenty of game remaining, New York scored seven unanswered points, fueled by the bench mob. Wednesday’s hero, Alvarado, scored five consecutive points, including a step-back three off his own offensive rebound, while Dadiet contributed a steal and a reverse layup off Brunson’s eighth assist to give the Knicks their first lead. Davion Mitchell finally broke Miami’s scoring drought with a floater, putting the Heat ahead 93-92 with six minutes remaining.

At the two-minute mark, the good guys trailed by three points after two freebies by Shamet. From there, Giannis launched an ill-advised, deep airball late in the shot clock; Brunson and Pelle Larsson traded free throws; Hart made one of two at the stripe; and Adebayo made the differential four with 44 seconds left. Captain Clutch’s floater made it 104-102. Giannis missed two free throws with 14 seconds on the clock, and Adebayo fouled Wiseman on the loose ball, giving our heroes a of hope. My bingo card did not have Wiseman shooting free throws with the game on the line. How about yours?

The young journeyman made one, missed one, and Giannis snagged the board and called a timeout. 104-103, 13 seconds to go. When play resumed, Dadiet fouled Mitchell, who made both attempts. On the Knicks’ inbounds play, the ball swung to Brunson in the corner, where he was fouled by Conwell. Even though Conwell violated JB’s landing space, Scott “The Enforcer” Foster deemed it a common foul. Cap made two of three at the line. Spoelstra called a timeout. 106-105, nine seconds.

Larsson got a breakaway dunk—on the exact same inbounds play the Heat had run on their previous possession. Mike Brown elected not to call a timeout, and Brunson missed a contested triple to end the game.

This is your recap, chaps. As for the Knicks, they’ll sleep in their own beds for a few more days and host the Hawks on Sunday. Rest up, troops.

title: Australia’s east coast deluged by storms as roads flood and damaging winds forecast for NSW and Victoria
author: Australian Associated Press
text:
Severe weather and flood watch warnings are in place as a storm band moves from central Queensland through NSW to Victoria and Tasmania

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

The final weekend of Australia’s wettest spring on record for an El Niño year is delivering a deluge of storms and heavy rain.

Severe weather and flood watch warnings were in place across the eastern states as a weather band moves from central Queensland through New South Wales to Victoria and Tasmania.

The Bureau of Meteorology’s Helen Reid said El Niño attracted great interest but was only one factor to consider when looking at a season and the continent in its entirety.

“El Niño is part of it, and we have had quite a lot of rainfall in the south-east but that’s … also a balance of what we didn’t have earlier in the winter season,” she said.

Tropical humidity has drifted across the continent and is being swept into the eastern states.

“We are looking at a very active system that’s going to be affecting southern Queensland, inland NSW, Victoria and also into Tasmania ,” Reid said.

Damaging winds were forecast for the NSW alpine region and Victoria’s central and eastern districts, which were also expecting heavy rainfall.

The heaviest overnight falls in Victoria were 85.4mm at Amphitheatre Reservoir in the northern Pyrenees region and 72.8mm at Bet Bet Creek in the state’s west.

Victorian State Emergency Service volunteers reported a busy 24 hours, with more than 340 calls for help to 6am on Saturday.

Most calls related to fallen trees (105), building damage (96) and flooding impacts (97).

The state’s north-east and eastern ranges can expect six-hourly rainfall totals from 55mm to 70mm on Saturday morning.

A moderate flood warning is in place for Warrill Creek in Queensland, with initial flood warnings in Tasmania for the Meander and Mersey rivers and flood watches for most of the catchments in western, central and north-east Victoria.

Meanwhile, a heatwave in the Northern Territory is easing but intensifying from severe to extreme in Western Australia’s Kimberley and Pilbara regions.

“It’s only going to be a shortlived heatwave but it is going to be a couple of hot days through there,” Reid said.

“Picking out Kununurra as an example, they’re looking at 42 or 43C for the next few days during the daytime but only dropping down to about 27C overnight.”

An offshore trough off WA’s coast would create a low-intensity heatwave stretching to just north of Perth.

Meanwhile, firefighting crews are facing another difficult day as they continue battling raging bushfires on Tasmania’s remote Flinders Island.

As other parts of Tasmania brace for heavy rains and potential flooding, crews on Flinders Island are battling a blaze that had burned 15,000 hectares by Friday - more than 10 per cent of the island.

Forecast heavy rainfall has yet to reach Flinders Island but Tasmania Fire Service incident controller Steven Richardson said it could create further challenges rather than provide relief.

“At this stage, the weather may actually create further challenges for firefighters on the ground, reducing our ability to strengthen containment lines through backburning and creating wet, slippery conditions,” he said.

“While some warnings have been downgraded, our crews are expecting another long day on the ground focusing on containment and asset protection.”

You’ll also find deals on Ember’s temperature-controlled mug , Kodak’s tiny keychain camera , and a variety of Lego sets , all of which would make great holiday gifts or simply a nice treat for yourself.

You can get an ad-supported Disney Plus and Hulu bundle for $4.99 a month ($8 off) for an entire year. Both streaming services feature a deep catalog of new and classic TV shows and movies, including The Simpsons , Andor , Toy Story 5 , and The Fantastic Four: First Steps .

Although it’s not Amazon’s first bedside alarm clock, the Echo Time is focused on helping you sleep better. The camera-less Alexa speaker can detect your sleep stage via ultrasound and use smart alarms to ease you into the day, but only if you want it to.

Anker’s durable travel adapter delivers up to 100W of power and works in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does offer a trio of USB-C ports and a nifty LCD display to keep tabs on the charge percentage.

An HBO Max Basic subscription provides access to shows like A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms , The Last of Us , and The Pitt , as well as films like Superman and Weapons . You can get a year of the monthly ad-supported subscription for $5.49 a month (about $6 off) until December 1st.

Noco’s Boost GB40 is a rechargeable battery with jumper cables to start six-liter gas or three-liter diesel engines. It also has USB ports so you can charge your phone, ensuring you always have a backup plan.

Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.

The Beats Studio Buds Plus sport an eye-catching translucent option and build upon the original with improved sound, better voice quality, and more effective ANC. They also include swappable silicone ear tips and support for native iOS and Android features. Read our review .

The Liene Pearl N200 Pro is a dye-sublimation photo printer that produces vivid, colorful prints for journals, scrapbooks, and more, with an easy-to-use companion app for customization. This particular bundle includes 50 sheets of photo paper and five ink cartridges, though refills are relatively affordable at around $25 for 50 sheets.

Peacock is a great way to catch up on a wealth of content from NBC’s various networks, whether you plan to rewatch The Office or catch up on all things Bravo. A Premium subscription also grants access to films from studios like Universal Pictures and DreamWorks, along with live sports and a host of Peacock Originals.

Do you ever wish you could turn on your coffee maker or hit the light switch without getting up? The SwitchBot Bot lets you do that. All you need to do is stick the inexpensive contraption on a standard button or rocker switch, which will allow you to control or schedule your pet feeder, garage door, and a wide range of other devices from your smartphone.

Ember’s latest smart mug is designed to keep your coffee at the ideal temperature for up to three hours, with five temp settings between 120 and 145 degrees Fahrenheit. The third-gen version is similar to prior models; however, you can now adjust the heat settings directly on the mug and throw it in the dishwasher, which wasn’t the case before.

Paramount Plus Premium provides access to live sports as well as movies and shows from both platforms, including Tales of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles , a host of Yellowston e spinoffs, Star Trek shows, Sonic the Hedgehog 3, Twin Peaks , Dexter , and more.

Apple’s entry-level stylus attaches magnetically to supported iPads, though it doesn’t support magnetic charging. Instead, you pair and charge it by connecting it to your device’s USB-C port. It includes tilt sensitivity and Apple Pencil Hover support, but it doesn’t offer double-tap gestures or pressure sensitivity.

The latest Beats Studio Pro feature improved noise cancellation, sound quality, and comfort. They also support lossless audio over USB-C and offer native support for a range of iOS and Android features like other Beats headphones. Read our review .

You likely won’t find wireless earbuds with a more striking appearance than Nothing’s Ear 3A. They also sound fantastic, boast active noise cancellation, and offer robust EQ settings, making them a great pick for the price. Read our review .

Rechargeable AA batteries are handy until it’s time to charge them. Most wall chargers let you refill four, maybe six, at once. Zepath’s clever solution is to ship them in an easy-to-use USB-C charging case that charges eight simultaneously. The batteries themselves are long-lasting, too.

The P9 is great if you need more storage for your Nintendo Switch 2. The microSD Express card offers sequential read speeds of up to 800MB/s, but only gadgets with a microSD Express card slot can take full advantage of the highest speeds. title: This purple electric Chinese minivan can go up to 559 miles on a charge
author: Sean Hollister
text:

The BYD Whale should cost around $45,000, not that you’d be able to buy one here.

Electric minivans could be the ultimate in utility, with room for passengers, gear, and huge batteries. While VW’s ID Buzz only gave us 200 miles of real-world driving on a charge in 2023 , China’s BYD has just announced a flagship purple peoplemover that can go an estimated 559 miles (900 km) on electricity.

It’s called the BYD Whale, and some back-of-the-napkin math suggests it lives up to the name. The van would be bigger than a Honda Odyssey, bigger than a Chrysler Pacifica, and bigger than a Toyota Sienna, at 17.3 feet (5,270mm) long, 6.5 feet (1,996mm) wide, 6 feet (1,815mm) tall, and with a 123-inch (3,130mm) wheelbase.

According to an auto-translated press release , the vehicle should have room for seven passengers and seven suitcases at a time, not that the company has shown off its interior yet. You can see a prominent sensor cluster on its forehead, though, and it’ll come equipped with LiDAR for advanced hands-free driving.

CarNewsChina points out it’s actually not the first with 900 km of CLTC battery range on board — Geely’s all electric Zeekr 009 minivan also claims to offer up to 900 km of range in one configuration. But BYD’s also claiming the can charge its battery from 10 percent to 97 percent in just nine minutes, and it get you from 10 percent to 70 percent in five minutes, according to Electrek .

The Whale will also come in a 248-mile (400 km) plug-in hybrid version as well, and the company’s planning to ship it in China in Q1 of 2027 for around 300,000 yuan. That’s roughly $45,000. As we’ve reported, Chinese cars are becoming quite competitive . Will they make it to the US?
